A B S T R A C T
High-temperature piezoelectric materials are essential for advanced sensor applications. However, it is chal-
lenging to achieve both high piezoelectric performance and a broad service temperature range. Aurivillius-type

lenging to achieve both high piezoelectric performance and a broad service temperature range. Aurivillius-type
bismuth layer-structured ferroelectric (BLSF) bismuth titanate-ferrite (Bi 5 Ti 3 FeO 15 ) has recently received sig-
nificant attention. However, the piezoelectric properties of Bi 5 Ti 3 FeO 15 -based compounds have not been
extensively explored due to their poor piezoelectric performance and low direct-current (dc) electrical resistivity
at elevated temperatures. To address these limitations, we optimized the composition by partially substituting A -
site bismuth ions with rare-earth ytterbium ions. This substitution aimed to enhance the piezoelectric perfor-
mance, dc electrical resistivity, and thermal stability of the piezoelectric properties. We conducted a detailed
examination of the crystal structure, microstructural morphology, and piezoelectric properties of ytterbium-
substituted Bi 5 Ti 3 FeO 15 . The optimal composition, 4 mol% ytterbium-substituted Bi 5 Ti 3 FeO 15 (BTF-4Yb), ex-

substituted Bi 5 Ti 3 FeO 15 . The optimal composition, 4 mol% ytterbium-substituted Bi 5 Ti 3 FeO 15 (BTF-4Yb), ex-
hibits a significantly improved piezoelectric constant ( d 33 ) of 21.4 pC/N, which is three times higher than that of
Bi 5 Ti 3 FeO 15 (7.1 pC/N). Additionally, it shows a high dc electrical resistivity of 1.6 M Ω cm at 400 C and a high
Curie temperature ( T C ) of 771 C. Importantly, BTF-4Yb maintains good thermal stability of electromechanical
coupling characteristics up to 300 C. These results indicate that ytterbium-substituted Bi 5 Ti 3 FeO 15 is a prom-
ising candidate for high-temperature piezoelectric ceramics, offering significant potential for applications in
high-temperature piezoelectric sensors.
1. Introduction
Piezoelectric materials, which convert electrical energy into me-
chanical energy, are highly sought after for piezoelectric applications
operating at elevated temperatures ( ≥ 300 ℃ ) to ensure structural

chanical energy, are highly sought after for piezoelectric applications
operating at elevated temperatures ( ≥ 300 ℃ ) to ensure structural
health monitoring and diagnostics in fields such as automotive, aero-
space, and power plants [1] . Currently, lead zirconate titanate (PZT)
piezoelectric ceramics with morphotropic phase boundary (MPB) com-
positions are the predominant choice due to their excellent electrome-
chanical coupling properties. However, PZT ceramics are unsuitable for
high-temperature applications due to their relatively low Curie tem-
perature ( T C < 400 ℃ ). Since piezoelectric materials can only be safely
used up to approximately half of their T C without significant perfor-
mance degradation, PZT ceramics are not viable for applications
exceeding 250 ℃ [2] . Aurivillius-type bismuth layer-structured ferro-
electrics (BLSFs), such as CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 (CBN) [3 – 6] , Bi 3 TiNbO 9 (BTN)

The general formula for BLSF oxides is (Bi 2 O 2 ) 2 + ( A m -1 B m O 3 m + 1 ) 2- , where
A represents monovalent, divalent, or trivalent metallic ions suitable for
dodecahedral coordination, B represents tetravalent, pentavalent, or
hexavalent transition metallic ions suitable for octahedral coordination,
and m ranges from 1 to 5, indicating the number of octahedral layers in
the perovskite slab [20 – 23] .

anisotropy [24] . Additionally, BLSFs often suffer from low electrical
resistivity, attributed to high concentrations of oxygen vacancies
resulting from the volatilization of bismuth during sintering [25,26] . To
address these limitations, researchers have explored various methods to
enhance the piezoelectric properties of BLSF compounds, such as
chemical doping and grain orientation techniques [27 – 29] .
Bismuth titanate-ferrite (Bi 5 Ti 3 FeO 15 , BTF) with m = 4 stands out in
the BLSF family as a promising high-temperature piezoelectric material,
due to its high T C (~761 C) [30] . While recent studies have focused on
the electromagnetic and ferromagnetic coupling applications of BTF,
there has been limited research on its piezoelectric properties. This is
largely attributed to the material ’ s rigid poling conditions, such as high
E c and significant leakage currents. Nevertheless, chemical modification
has proven to be a cost-effective strategy for simultaneously enhancing

E c and significant leakage currents. Nevertheless, chemical modification
has proven to be a cost-effective strategy for simultaneously enhancing
the piezoelectric properties and electrical resistivity of BTF, paving the
way for large-scale manufacturing. For example, Moure et al. reported
an enhanced d 33 of 18.6 pC/N in Bi 5 Ti 3 FeO 15 -CaBi 4 Ti 4 O 15 (BTF-CBT)
[31] ; Huang et al. achieved a d 33 of 13.4 pC/N in (Na, Ce) co-modified
BTF [32] ; and Wang et al. attained a high d 33 of 23 pC/N in Mn-modified
BTF [30] .
However, there is a paucity of studies on the effects of A -site rare-
earth ion substitutions on the piezoelectric properties and thermal sta-
bility of BTF. In this study, we propose a strategy involving A -site sub-
stitution with ytterbium (Yb) to stabilize the (Bi 2 O 2 ) 2 + layer and reduce
the concentration of oxygen vacancies. This approach aims to enhance
both the piezoelectric properties and thermal stability of BTF. We

the concentration of oxygen vacancies. This approach aims to enhance
both the piezoelectric properties and thermal stability of BTF. We
thoroughly investigate the structure, dielectric, electrical, piezoelectric,
and electromechanical properties of A -site ytterbium-substituted BTF.
2. Experimental procedure
Ytterbium-substituted Bi 5 Ti 3 FeO 15 with nominal compositions of
Bi 5- x Yb x Ti 3 FeO 15 (abbreviated as BTF-100 x Yb, where x = 0.00, 0.02,
0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.10, 0.15, and 0.20) were fabricated using the con-
ventional solid-state reaction method. Analytical grade Bi 2 O 3 (99.80 %),
TiO 2 (99.80 %), Fe 2 O 3 (99.40 %), and Yb 2 O 3 (99.99 %) were used as raw
materials and weighed in stoichiometric ratios. The raw materials were
mixed and milled with ZrO 2 balls in ethanol for 12 h. After drying, the
mixture was calcined at 750 C for 3 h to synthesize the target product.
The calcined mixture was then ground, milled, and dried again under

mixture was calcined at 750 C for 3 h to synthesize the target product.
The calcined mixture was then ground, milled, and dried again under
the same conditions. The resulting powder was granulated with poly-
vinyl alcohol (PVA) binders and pressed into disks 12 mm in diameter
and 1.0 mm in thickness. Finally, each disk was heated at 650 C to burn
off the PVA binder and then sintered at 1050 – 1060 C for 3 h at a heating
rate of 3 C/min in an aluminum oxide crucible to prepare the
ytterbium-substituted BTF ceramic samples.
The structural analysis of the prepared powders was conducted using
an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Smartlab SE; Rigaku Corporation) with
Cu K α radiation. Raman spectra of the samples were obtained using a
Raman spectrometer (LabRAM HR 800, HORIBA Jobin-Yvon) with a He-
Ne laser (632.8 nm). Natural surface micrographs were captured using a
field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, Merlin FE-SEM;
Carl Zeiss). Prior to measuring electrical properties, silver electrodes

field-emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, Merlin FE-SEM;
Carl Zeiss). Prior to measuring electrical properties, silver electrodes
were screen-printed on both surfaces of polished samples and fired at
570 C for 20 min. Dielectric properties and resonance response were
measured using an impedance analyzer (E4990A; Keysight Technolo-
gies) equipped with a multimeter (Keithley 2000; Tektronix). Electrical
resistivity was calculated from resistance measurements taken by a
source meter (Keithley 2410; Tektronix Inc.) with a voltage of 100 V
applied to the sample. Ferroelectric hysteresis loops were obtained using
a TF 2000E Analyzer (aixACCT Systems GmbH, Germany). The piezo-
electric constant d 33 was measured using a YE2730A d 33 meter after the
samples were poled in silicone oil under a direct-current (dc) electric
field of 60 – 70 kV/cm at 150 C for 20 min.

Compared with X-ray diffraction (XRD), Raman scattering is not only
more sensitive and efficient for investigating lattice vibration modes but
also provides more detailed information related to the crystallographic
positions of substitutional ions and their effects on ferroelectric behavior
through the occurrence of extra modes and/or shifts in peak position
[36] . Fig. 2 presents Raman scattering spectra with Raman shifts ranging
from 50 to 1000 cm − 1 at room temperature. Generally, the Raman
spectra of Aurivillius-type materials can be categorized into two types of
phonon modes [37] . The first type includes modes with frequencies
below 200 cm − 1 , which are associated with the vibrations of Bi atoms at
the A -site. The second type includes modes with frequencies above
200 cm − 1 , related to the internal vibrations of oxygen octahedra in the
perovskite-like layers. In the BTF ceramic samples, prominent Raman
modes appear at around 100, 116, 142, 230, 261, 333, 539, 571, and

860 cm − 1 , indicating the formation of a well-defined four-layer perov-
skite structure. The low-frequency Raman modes near 100, 116, and
142 cm − 1 are closely related to the vibrations of Bi 3 + ions at the A -site of
the perovskite-like slabs [38] . The high-frequency Raman modes around
230 and 261 cm − 1 correspond to the bending vibrations of the
O-Ti/Fe-O bonds in the oxygen octahedron [39] . Raman modes near
333 cm − 1 are associated with the combined twisting and stretching vi-
brations of the oxygen octahedron [40] , while the modes around 539
and 571 cm − 1 are related to the relative vibrations of the oxygen atom at
the top outer end of the (Ti/Fe)O 6 octahedron [41] . The high-frequency
mode appearing around 860 cm − 1 corresponds to the tensile vibrations
of the TiO 6 octahedron along the c -axis [42] .
After the introduction of ytterbium ions, the characteristic peaks
mentioned above remain evident, suggesting that the ytterbium substi-

of the TiO 6 octahedron along the c -axis [42] .
After the introduction of ytterbium ions, the characteristic peaks
mentioned above remain evident, suggesting that the ytterbium substi-
tution does not significantly alter the basic structure of BTF. Notably, the
high-frequency Raman modes located near 230 and 333 cm − 1 are
intensified compared to the BTF, indicating the effect of ytterbium
substitution on the distortion of the (Ti/Fe)O 6 octahedron. This also
suggests that ytterbium ions tend to replace bismuth ions, affecting the
local structural environment around the B O 6 octahedron, including
changes in the phonon vibration frequency of the outer oxygen atom at
the top of the (Ti/Fe)O 6 octahedron and a reduction in local structural
symmetry. Additionally, the positions and intensities of other Raman
peaks show little change, indicating they are not significantly affected
by the ytterbium ion replacement of bismuth ions.

compact, pore-free microstructure, indicating optimal sintering condi-

developed, laminar, and randomly oriented, characteristic of BLSF ce-

c -axis of BLSF crystals, the grain growth is structurally anisotropic, with
the length of the plate-like grains significantly exceeding their thickness.
Compared to BTF, the ytterbium-substituted BTF ceramics exhibit larger
grain sizes, which are advantageous for enhancing piezoelectric prop-
erties [44] . The average grain size of BTF increases significantly with
increasing ytterbium content, demonstrating that the substitution of
ytterbium improves mass diffusion and accelerates the migration of ions
during the sintering process [21] , thus facilitating the grain growth. This
observation is consistent with recent reports on other BLSF compounds

High dc electrical resistivity at elevated temperatures is crucial for
the practical application of piezoelectric ceramics. Ceramics with low
electrical resistivity can generate high leakage currents, leading to
charge drift and interference with the detection of charges induced by
the piezoelectric effect [46] . Fig. 4 (a) shows the temperature depen-
dence of the dc electrical resistivity of BTF-100 x Yb ceramics. The dc
resistivity gradually decreases with increasing temperature, indicating a
thermally activated process with a negative temperature coefficient of
dc electrical resistance. As shown in Table 2 , the maximum resistivity
values are observed for BTF-4Yb, measuring 2.4 × 10 7 Ω cm at 300 C,
1.6 × 10 6 Ω cm at 400 C, and 1.8 × 10 5 Ω cm at 500 C. These values are
higher than those of BTF, which are 8.8 × 10 6 Ω cm at 300 ℃ , 5.6 × 10 5 Ω

1.6 × 10 6 Ω cm at 400 C, and 1.8 × 10 5 Ω cm at 500 C. These values are
higher than those of BTF, which are 8.8 × 10 6 Ω cm at 300 ℃ , 5.6 × 10 5 Ω
cm at 400 ℃ , and 6.7 × 10 4 Ω cm at 500 ℃ . The high dc electrical re-
sistivity allows ytterbium-substituted BTF ceramics to withstand higher
electric fields, enhancing their piezoelectric properties through suffi-
cient polarization. Several factors may contribute to the change in dc
resistivity with different levels of ytterbium substitution. The (Bi 2 O 2 ) 2 +

Aurivillius-type compounds, improving electrical properties by sup-
pressing leakage currents [47] . Bismuth ions tend to volatilize during
high-temperature sintering due to its relatively low melting point (~820
C), leading to the formation of oxygen vacancies that act as charge
carriers [48] . The substitution of the highly volatile bismuth ions with
ytterbium ions, which have a higher melting point (~2346 C), can

carriers [48] . The substitution of the highly volatile bismuth ions with
ytterbium ions, which have a higher melting point (~2346 C), can
effectively suppress bismuth loss during sintering. This stabilization of

the (Bi 2 O 2 ) 2 + layers reduced the formation of point defects such as ox-
ygen vacancies. Another contributing factor is the change in grain
morphology due to ytterbium modifications. In Aurivillius-type mate-
rials, grain growth is structurally anisotropic, occurring primarily in the
a - b plane, while the (Bi 2 O 2 ) 2 + layers along the c -axis act as natural
insulating media. Larger grain sizes in ytterbium-substituted ceramics
facilitate long-range charge transport due to reduced grain boundary
effects and weaker insulation by the (Bi 2 O 2 ) 2 + layers [8] . This explains
why the resistivity decreases with increasing ytterbium substitution,
particularly in BTF-20Yb.

and thereby increasing the contribution of defect-induced losses. With
the combination of these two mechanisms, the dielectric loss increased
with more ytterbium substitutions as the temperature increases. How-
ever, the dielectric loss of BTF-4Yb ceramics is lower than 0.03 below

scenarios.

4. Conclusion
Bismuth layer-structured ferroelectric Bi 5 Ti 3 FeO 15 ceramics with
rare-earth ytterbium ion substitutions were synthesized using the con-
ventional solid-state reaction method. We thoroughly investigated the
structural, dielectric, electrical, piezoelectric, and electromechanical
properties of A -site ytterbium-substituted Bi 5 Ti 3 FeO 15 . The piezoelectric
constant ( d 33 ) was significantly enhanced by substituting ytterbium ions
for bismuth ions, with BTF-4Yb exhibiting the optimal piezoelectric
performance ( d 33 = 21.4 pC/N), which is three times greater than that of
BTF. The Curie temperature ( T C ) values slightly increased with higher
ytterbium content due to the lattice distortion of the BTF caused by
substituting
smaller

ytterbium

among all the compositions. The thermal annealing behavior of BTF-

have potential for high-temperature applications. Additionally, the
temperature-dependent electrical impedance, resonance frequency, and
anti-resonance frequency measurements show that BTF-4Yb maintains
good thermal stability of electromechanical properties. These findings
suggest that ytterbium-substituted BTF ceramics are promising materials
for high-temperature piezoelectric applications.

A B S T R A C T
Bi Ti O (BIT), a typical Aurivillius ceramics with high Curie temperature ( T ˜ 675 °C), has great potential for
high temperature applications. This work provides an e ﬀ ective method of inducing structure distortion, relieving
the tetragonal strain of the TiO octahedron and decreasing the concentration of oxygen vacancies to improve
the piezoelectricity and temperature stability of BIT ceramics. Bi Ti W Nb O possesses an optimum
piezoelectric coe ﬃ cient ( d ) of 32 pC/N, a high T of 655 °C and a large resistivity of 3 × 10 Ω ·cm at 500 °C.

1. Introduction
Aurivillius ferroelectrics (bismuth layer structure ferroelectrics,
BLSFs) have attracted much attention owing to their high Curie tem-
perature ( T ), good temperature stability and excellent fatigue-resistant
properties [ 1 – 4 ]. Consequently, BLSFs ceramics display excellent po-
tential for applications in high temperature piezoelectric sensor systems
and nonvolatile ferroelectric random-access memories (Nv RAMs)
[ 5 , 6 ]. The general chemical formula of BLSFs is (Bi O ) (A
B O ) , and its structure is an intergrowth of (A B O )

and nonvolatile ferroelectric random-access memories (Nv RAMs)
[ 5 , 6 ]. The general chemical formula of BLSFs is (Bi O ) (A
B O ) , and its structure is an intergrowth of (A B O )
units and (Bi O ) slabs along the c -axis, where the A sites are larger
cations (Na , K , Ca , Sr , Bi etc .) and the B sites are smaller
cations (Ti , Nb , V , Mo , W etc .), with n (1 ≤ n ≤ 6) the
number of oxygen octahedra in the pseudo-perovskite layers.
Bi Ti O (BIT, n = 3), the prototype of BLSFs, is identi ﬁ ed as a
desirable candidate for application in the high temperature environ-
ment because of its high T ( ˜ 675 °C) and large ferroelectric polarization
[ 7 ]. The spontaneous polarization ( P ) of BIT single crystals along the a -
axis can be as high as approximately 50 μ C/cm [ 8 ]. However, the
piezoelectric coe ﬃ cient ( d ) of BIT is relatively low ( ˜ 8 pC/N) due to
its large coercive ﬁ eld ( E ) [ 9 , 10 ]. Furthermore, BIT presents typical p -

piezoelectric coe ﬃ cient ( d ) of BIT is relatively low ( ˜ 8 pC/N) due to
its large coercive ﬁ eld ( E ) [ 9 , 10 ]. Furthermore, BIT presents typical p -
type electrical conduction owning to Bi evaporation during sintering,
which results in its very high electrical conductivity [ 11 , 12 ]. Therefore,
the low piezoelectric activity and high electrical conductivity represent
the dominant bottlenecks restricting the application of BIT ceramics.
It ’ s has been demonstrated that B site co-doped BIT-based ceramics by
high valence cations substitution is an e ﬀ ective approach to enhance
the electrical properties and decrease the concentration of defects. Hou
et al. reported that a larger piezoelectric coe ﬃ cient ( d ) of 26 pC/N
could be obtained by Nb/Ta modi ﬁ cation at the B-site for BIT ceramics,
owing to the TiO deformation and decrease of oxygen vacancies [ 13 ].

Though much progress has been made in recent years to improve
the piezoelectric properties of BIT ceramics, the piezoelectric properties
and temperature stability of BIT-based ceramics are still not su ﬃ cient
to ensure excellent operational reliability at elevated temperatures.
Therefore, it is still of vital importance to further enhance the piezo-
electric properties of Bi Ti O ceramics and its temperature stability.
More importantly, high-temperature resistivity characteristics, as key
factors for high-temperature application, need to be systematically in-
vestigated. Unfortunately, up to now only few reports are concerned
with the reliability evaluation of the designed sensor fabricated with
BIT-based ceramics at high temperature, which is of equal importance.

Based on the p -type conduction mechanism of many BLSF ceramics,
it can be expected that the resistivity can be increased by donor doping
and that good piezoelectric properties can be achieved via su ﬃ cient
polarization. For example, Na Bi Ti O -based ceramics with B-site
substitution show excellent piezoelectric properties ( d = 28 pC/N)
with W/Nb co-doping [ 17 ]. Therefore, donor doping is expected to
enhance electrical properties of BIT ceramics and further investigation
of B site W/Nb-modi ﬁ ed BIT-based ceramics is also of interest. In this
work, we report signi ﬁ cantly enhanced piezoelectric properties and
temperature stability of BIT ceramics with B-site substitution using W/
Nb ions by a solid solution reaction method. To clarifying the e ﬀ ects of
W/Nb substitution on BIT ceramics, their structure characteristics, di-

Introduction
Electromechanical transducing materials are required to sense
strains, vibrations and noise under severe thermal conditions.
Among the different types of acoustic and strain sensors, piezo-
electrics are the best candidates when one considers sensitivity,
cost and design. Piezoelectric single crystals such as LiNbO ,
GaPO , La Ga SiO , Sr Nb O , YCa O(BO ) , GdCa O(BO ) and
A Ti O (A = Nd and La) are generally used as high-temperature
sensing components. However, the crystal growth of these
materials needs expensive equipment and has a low yield. An
important advantage of piezoelectric ceramics over single crys-
tals is the ease with which the composition and properties may
be tailored. Aurivillius ferroelectrics (bismuth layer-structured
ferroelectrics, BLSFs) have received much attention for their
potential use in high-temperature piezoelectric devices, owing
to their relatively high Curie temperature T . Modified and
high-energy mechanochemical technique prepared bismuth

potential use in high-temperature piezoelectric devices, owing
to their relatively high Curie temperature T . Modified and
high-energy mechanochemical technique prepared bismuth
titanate (Bi Ti O , BiT) ceramics are interesting for sensor
applications up to 500 ° C. When an operating temperature is
needed to be up to 800 ° C, the choice of piezoelectric materials
is limited. Among pure Aurivillius oxides, only two-layer
CaBi Me O and Bi TiMeO (Me = Nb, Ta), have ultra-high
T ( > 850 ° C), between 870 and 943 ° C. However, their piezoelectric

owing to the two-dimensional orientation restriction of the
reversal of spontaneous polarization as well as the high coer-
cive field ( E ). With a grain orientation technique of spark
plasma sintering (SPS), the textured CaBi Nb O (CBNO)
ceramic had a higher d of 19.5 pC N , which is nearly three
times that of the ordinarily fired samples (OF). For two-layer

Experimental
Appropriate amounts of starting the materials [Bi O (99.5%),
Nb O (99.5%), CaCO (99.8%), Nd O (99.99%), Li CO (99.99%),
WO (99.99%) and Sc O (99.99%); Sinopharm Chemical
Reagent Co., Ltd, CN] were mixed by a ball milling method in

WO (99.99%) and Sc O (99.99%); Sinopharm Chemical

ethanol for 24 h. The mixtures were dried and then calcined

Conclusions
Modified ultrahigh-temperature piezoelectrics, Ca Li Nd
□ Bi Nb Sc W O (CBNO-LiNd-ScW- x , x = 0, 0.01, 0.02,
0.03, 0.04; □ represented A-site vacancies), were synthesized
by a traditional solid-state reaction process, where Li /Nd
and Sc /W co-substituted the A-site Ca and B-site Nb ,
respectively, as well as the presence of small amounts of A-site
vacancies. The structures and domain structures of the pre-
pared ceramics were characterized by using XRD, SEM TEM,
HRTEM and Raman spectroscopy. More A-site cations are
involved in the (Bi O ) layers, which led to a drop in the T
in CBNO-LiNd-ScW- x , from 941 ° C to 832 ° C. A lower level
modification ( x = 0.01) gave rise to an enhancement in the
electro-mechanical properties as well as the ferroelectric
properties, due to the perfect growth in the ferroelectric
domains and the contribution from the reversal of the defect
dipoles (V ″– V
and Sc ″– V
). With a higher level
acceptor substitution, a degradation in d , S and P was

domains and the contribution from the reversal of the defect
dipoles (V ″– V
and Sc ″– V
). With a higher level
acceptor substitution, a degradation in d , S and P was
observed in CBNO-LiNd-ScW- x ( x = 0.02 – 0.04), which could be
attributed to the “ pinning ” effect of the oxygen vacancies on
the domain walls and a dimensional mismatch between the
perovskite and bismuth oxide layer. The CBNO-LiNd-ScW-0.01
ceramic with an ultrahigh T of 908 ° C had a high piezoelec-
tric activity ( d ) of 20.6 pC N , a large field-induced strain
( S ) of 0.27 × 10 and a high P of 6.1 μ C cm ; interestingly,
it still has high d of 19.5 pC N after up to 800 ° C thermal
annealing. In addition, the CBNO-LiNd-ScW-0.01 ceramic
had relatively high resistivity of > 10 Ω cm at 600 ° C and
> 10 Ω cm at 700 ° C. Therefore, the CBNO-LiNd-ScW-0.01
ceramic would be a promising candidate for use as an ultrahigh-
temperature piezoelectric.

1. Introduction
Environment friendly perovskite structure piezoelectric ceramics
have been intensively studied in recent years [1 , 2 ]. However, the low
Curie temperature limits their applications in some hazardous envir-
onments.

bismuth

CaBi Nb O (CBN) material, a typical two-layered Aurivillius
type compound, possesses the known high Curie temperature
( ∼ 930 1 C) and thermal depoling temperature for polycrystalline
ceramics [5 , 6 ]. However, the piezoelectric coef ﬁ cient d of pure
CBN ceramic is relatively low ( ∼ 7 pC/N). Many investigations have
been carried out to improve the piezoelectric properties including
texturing techniques and/or chemical modi ﬁ cations. It was an
effective way to improve the piezoelectric properties using rare-
earth elements La and/or Ce dopants but degraded the T
value [7 – 9 ]. The d value was signi ﬁ cantly improved to be
∼ 17.8 pC/N via grain orientation techniques, and the T value was
not affected [6] . On the other hand, it has been reported that

In the present paper, we focus on the effects of (LiCePr)-
multimodi ﬁ ed CBN ceramics prepared by the mixed oxide routes.
The crystal structure, dielectric behavior and piezoelectric proper-
ties were investigated. Furthermore, the thermal depoling beha-
vior and electrical impedance modulus at elevated temperatures
were also addressed.

effectively promote the d of CaBi Nb O (CBN), its thermal depoling behavior

lattice evolution from orthorhombic structure to pseudo-tetragonal structure during
thermal depoling process. A-site vacancies could induce pseudo-tetragonal distor-
tion in Ca (Na Ce ) Bi Nb O ceramic, which obviously enhanced the
thermal stability of lattice by reducing the rotation of the Nb – O octahedron during

weakening the swing of spontaneous polarization ( P ) and promoting the thermal

mained 92% of initial d after depoling at 600 ° C). Moreover, dominant role of
oxygen vacancies in the electrical conduction and relaxation process promised that
the introduction of small amount of A-site vacancies would not influence the elec-

morphotropic phase boundary (MPB). Taking environ-
mental and human health into consideration, lead-free ceram-

obtain excellent electric properties via regulating phase

higher than 450 ° C, the comparatively low Curie temperature

depolarization at around 100 ° C ( T ) for BNT restrict their
possible use in high-temperature applications.

EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE
Samples of compositions Ca (Na □ Ce ) Bi Nb O
(abbreviated as CBNNC-V100 x , x = 0-0.20 with an interval
of 0.05) were prepared by a conventional solid-state reaction
method. The weighted raw materials of Bi O (99.9%),
CaCO (99%), Nb O (99.9%), Na CO (99.8%), and CeO
(99.99%) were mixed by planetary mill for 24 hours. Calcina-
tion of the milled powders was carried out at 850 ° C for
4 hours in air, and then these mixtures were milled again in
the same condition. After drying, the powders were mixed
thoroughly with a PVA binder solution, and then pressed into
disks with a pressure of 10 MPa. Finally, the disks were sin-
tering at 1120 ° C for 4 hours. For electrical measurement, the
sintered ceramics were coated with silver paste to form elec-
trodes on both sides and fired at 650 ° C for 10 minutes. The
samples were poled at 180 ° C in the silicon oil bath by apply-
ing dc electric field of 9-10 kV/mm for 10 minutes.
The crystal structures for all samples were characterized

Piezoelectric constant ( d ) and its thermal stability are

wide range of temperature. Figure 4 shows the d values
of CBNNC-V100 x ceramics and their thermal depoling

of ceramics is also promoted dramatically via introducing
vacancy. The samples with pseudo-tetragonal structure
( x = 0.10-0.20) exhibit better thermal depoling performance
than orthorhombic structure ( x = 0, 0.05). When annealing
temperature elevates to 600 ° C, CBNNC-V15 remains 92%
of its initial value with d of 14.8 pC/N, which is much
larger than the 79% with 11.9 pC/N of CBNNC-V0.

lattice parameters of the orthorhombic structure are a , b

rise to orthorhombic structure and lower a / b gives rise to
tetragonal structure. There exists a positive correlation
between lattice parameters and temperature, and both lat-

of temperature, which induces the decrease in a / b and gives
rise to tetragonal structure. The refinement curves are also
given in Figure 6, and the values of reliability factors Sig
and Rw are in reasonable range.

CONCLUSIONS
Thermal instability of Ca (Na Ce ) Bi Nb O cera-
mic was caused by the lattice evolution from orthorhombic
structure
to
pseudo-tetragonal
structure
during thermal
depoling process. The introduction of A-site vacancies-
induced
pseudo-tetragonal
distortion
in
Ca (Na
Ce ) Bi Nb O ceramic, which enhanced its thermal
stability via reducing the rotation of the Nb – O octahedron
during the thermal depoling process, thereby weakening the
swing of spontaneous polarization ( P ) and promoting the
thermal depoling performance. Consequently, CBNNC-V15
with pseudo-tetragonal structure remained 92% of initial d
after depoling at 600 ° C, much better than 79% of CBNNC-
V0 with orthorhombic structure. Moreover, the dominant
role of oxygen vacancies in electrical conduction and relax-
ation process ensured that the introduction of small amount
of A-site vacancies would not influence the electrical prop-
erties obviously. This work may provide a new viewpoint

ceramics. The crystal structure, microstructure, and electric properties of CBNCW- x ceramics have been
systematically analyzed. The results show that ceramic samples have a bismuth layered structure of m = 2,
which is a single-phase of CBN. The ceramic grains show the typical plate-like structure of the bismuth
layer. Cu/W co-doped CBN ceramics increased the distortion of NbO octahedron, and significantly en­
hanced the piezoelectric constant and the remnant polarization. When x = 0.075, it shows better com­
prehensive properties with an excellent d of 13.8 pC/N, a high remnant polarization of 12.10 μ C/cm , the T
of 918 °C, a dielectric loss value of 0.57%, and the Q value of 7099. Moreover, CBNCW-0.075 ceramic simple
maintains the d of 12.7 pC/N after annealing 900 °C for 30 min, which shows good high-temperature

1. Introduction
At present, the widely used piezoelectric material is PZT-based
piezoelectric ceramics, but its Curie temperature is low ( T < 400 °C),
and it is a Pb-containing material, which cannot be used normally in
a high-temperature environment [1–8] . Therefore, it is necessary to
explore piezoelectric materials that are more suitable for high-
temperature environments.
Bismuth layered structure compounds (BLSFs) are important
high-temperature lead-free piezoelectric ceramic materials. They
have the advantages of high Curie temperature ( T > 500 °C), good
thermal stability, and high quality factor, which shows a certain
potential for high-temperature applications. The chemical formula

tahedral pseudo-perovskite layers, generally between 1 and 5; A is
+ 1, + 2, + 3 valence ions or twelve-coordinated ion groups; B is a six-
coordinated transition metal ion [7] . Due to the alternating ar­
rangement of the (Bi O ) layer and the ( A B O ) layer, the
rotation of the spontaneous polarization ( P ) is restricted to the a - b
plane, resulting in a relatively low piezoelectric performance [9–11] .
Since there is almost no displacement of the lattice sites along the c -
axis, the contribution of the piezoelectric and ferroelectric for the
BLSFs comes from the tilt of the oxygen octahedron along the a - b
plane [9] . Reports have shown that the remnant polarization can be
significantly increased by increasing the oxygen octahedral distor­

will cause Bi O to volatilize during the high-temperature sintering
process, causing structural defects and further deterioration of its
electrical properties.

2. Experimental process
Cuprum and tungsten co-doped CaBi Nb O ceramics with che­
mical formula Ca Bi Nb (Cu W ) O (CBNCW- x , x = 0.000, 0.025,
0.075, 0.125, and 0.150) were prepared by conventional ceramic sin­
tering process using high-purity raw materials [Bi O (99.999%),
CaCO (99%), Nb O (99.5%), CuO(99%), WO (99.99%)]. The raw mate­
rials were weighed and mixed in a nylon jar with high-purity alcohol
for 24 h. The dried mixture was calcined at 750 °C for 3 h and then re-

rials were weighed and mixed in a nylon jar with high-purity alcohol
for 24 h. The dried mixture was calcined at 750 °C for 3 h and then re-
milled for 24 h. After drying, the powders were granulated with
polyvinyl alcohol (PVA, 5 wt %) binder, and then aged for 24 h. Disks
with a diameter of 13 mm and thickness of 1 mm were formed by
pressing at 300 ± 20 MPa, then burned out the PVA at 650 °C for 2.5 h.
The pressed pellets were sintered between 1030 and 1150 °C for 2 h
with 5 °C/min. The sintered ceramics were polished to about 0.5 mm
thick, and then painted with Ag/Pd paste and fired at 800 °C for 10 min
with 10 °C/min. The ceramics were poled in silicone oil at 180 °C for
30 min with a direct-current electric field of 200–260 kV/cm.
The XRD patterns of the sintered ceramics were determined at
room temperature using an X-ray diffractometer (D8 Advanced
Germany) equipped with Cu-K α radiation. The Raman spectra were
measured at room temperature by a Raman spectrometer (LabRAM

room temperature using an X-ray diffractometer (D8 Advanced
Germany) equipped with Cu-K α radiation. The Raman spectra were
measured at room temperature by a Raman spectrometer (LabRAM
HR800) equipped with a laser of 532 nm wavelength. The micro­
structure of the sintered ceramics with thermally etched was char­
acterized by a field-emission scanning electron microscope (SU8010,
Japan). The temperature dependence of dielectric constant and loss
of ceramics was measured by an LCR analyzer (TH2828s, Tong Hui,
China). The ferroelectric hysteresis of ceramics was measured at
10 Hz by using a ferroelectric meter (TRek model 609B). The pie­
zoelectric constants of ceramics were measured by using a quasi-
static d meter (ZJ-3A, China). The resonance frequency ( f ) and
antiresonance frequency ( f ) of polarized ceramics were determined
by using an LCR analyzer (HP4294A, Agilent, US).

4. Conclusion
The CBNCW- x ceramic samples were prepared by the traditional
solid-phase method. All the samples were of a single CBN crystal
structure, and the ceramic grains grew well and showed a typical
bismuth layered plate-like structure. Cu/W ions doping reduces the
degree of orthogonal distortion of CBN ceramics, but an appropriate
doping amount can effectively increase the distortion of NbO oc­
tahedrons in pseudo-perovskite. In addition, Cu/W doping still
shows the effects of additives of CuO, such as effectively reducing
the sintering temperature, reducing dielectric loss, and improving
quality factor. When the doping amount x ≥ 0.125, the internal ions

the sintering temperature, reducing dielectric loss, and improving
quality factor. When the doping amount x ≥ 0.125, the internal ions
are disordered, the relaxation degree increases and the electrical
properties decrease rapidly. Therefore, an appropriate amount of
doping can greatly improve the piezoelectric and ferroelectric
properties while maintaining a high Curie temperature. The high-
temperature stability test of all samples performed well. When the
doping amount x = 0.075, the comprehensive performance of CBN
ceramics reaches the best: d = 13.8 pC/N, P = 12.10 μ C/cm ,

Abstract
CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 (CBN), one of the bismuth-layered structural ferroelectrics, with
high Curie temperature ( T C ), has great potential in high-temperature applica-
tions. In this work, high Curie temperature and piezoelectric constant ( d 33 ) are
realized in modified CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ceramics with Ce-substitution. Ce-substitution
changes the crystal structures and domain structures of CBN-based ceram-
ics, so as to improve the piezoelectric properties. The optimal performances
are obtained with a high d 33 value ( ∼ 18.0 pC/N) and a T C value ( ∼ 930 ◦ C),
together with a low tan δ value ( ∼ 0.028 at 500 ◦ C). Moreover, the thermal sta-
bility is also enhanced, where the d 33 value maintains 93.9% of its original
value after annealing at 900 ◦ C for 2 h. Thus, these findings play a meaningful
role in devices manufacturing, where the apply temperature is often more than
500 ◦ C.

INTRODUCTION
Piezoelectric acceleration sensors, as function of vibra-
tion test calibration, mechanical dynamic experiment,
environmental simulation test, and fault diagnosis, are
widely employed in nuclear power industry, oil produc-
tion, aerospace, and so forth. 1 As is known, the working
temperatures in these fields usually exceed 600 ◦ C, some
of which even reach 1000 ◦ C, with more strict demands
for the performances of sensors. 1,2 From the perspective
of applications, the materials for sensors ought to have
following characteristics: (1) good piezoelectric properties
to guarantee sensitivity of sensors, (2) high T C values
to ensure that the service temperature of piezoelectric
materials is high enough, which is always lower than
half of Curie temperature accounting for the depolar-
ization effect of ferroelectrics, (3) stable piezoelectric
performance and large resistivity at high temperature
to let engines run steadily for long time under a high-
temperature
condition.
Therefore,
the

CBN ceramics ( m = 2) with highest T C values (about
940 ◦ C), have enormous potential for high-temperature
industries. 4 Nevertheless, the piezoelectric constant of
pure CBN ceramic is ∼ 6.0 pC/N, 5 which heavily lim-
its the sensitivity of devices. Hence, it is necessary to
improve piezoelectric properties of BLSFs to satisfy devices
applications.
As is known, the d 33 value of BLSFs is poor because
the spontaneous polarization is confined to the a – b plane
other than the vertical direction. Both chemical doping and
processing improvement can lead to structural distortion
and thus improve the piezoelectric constant. For example,
Liu et al. prepared Ca 0.92 (Na 0.5 Ce 0.5 ) 0.08 Bi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ceram-
ics, demonstrating a high d 33 value of 16.1 pC/N and good
thermal stability, 6 with a high d 33 value ( ∼ 17.6 pC/N) and a
relative low T C value ( ∼ 904 ◦ C) in Na/Bi/Li/Ce-doped CBN

thermal stability, 6 with a high d 33 value ( ∼ 17.6 pC/N) and a
relative low T C value ( ∼ 904 ◦ C) in Na/Bi/Li/Ce-doped CBN
ceramics. 7 In addition, B-site co-substitution CBN ceram-
ics such as MoCr, WCr, and WCu also exhibited improved
d 33 values to 15.0, 15.0, and 14.0 pC/N, respectively. 8–10
Among them, the substitution of A-sites is a feasible way to
improve piezoelectric properties of CBN-based ceramics.
However, how to simultaneously achieve good piezoelec-
tric properties and a high T C value of CBN-based ceramic
is desired to devote efforts at present.
In general, a d 33 value is negatively correlated with a T C
value in other reports. 6,8,9 Previously, it was reported that
the CBN-based ceramic exhibits a high T C value ( ∼ 947 ◦ C)
and excellent resistance performance ( ∼ 1.53 × 10 6 Ω cm
at 600 ◦ C) but a poor d 33 value ( ∼ 13.0 pC/N) by intro-
ducing Gd ion at A-site. 11 Based on (Li/Ce, X) co-doping

and excellent resistance performance ( ∼ 1.53 × 10 6 Ω cm
at 600 ◦ C) but a poor d 33 value ( ∼ 13.0 pC/N) by intro-
ducing Gd ion at A-site. 11 Based on (Li/Ce, X) co-doping
at A-site, CBN-based ceramics show high d 33 values of
17.2, 17.3, and 17.0 pC/N for X = Bi, Pr, Y, 5,12,13 respec-
tively, indicating the potentiality of improving d 33 values
via Li/Ce ions. Therefore, Ce, Li, and Gd ions are adopted
to improve the performances of CBN-based ceramic. In
this work, Ca 0.86 (LiGd 1 − x Ce x ) 0.07 Bi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ceramics are
prepared by a traditional solid-state method. Their struc-
tures, electrical properties, piezoelectric properties, and
so forth are studied. Finally, the ceramics with the for-
mula Ca 0.86 (LiGd 0.6 Ce 0.4 ) 0.07 Bi 2 Nb 2 O 9 exhibits enhanced
piezoelectric properties ( d 33 ∼ 18.0 pC/N), high T C val-
ues, and good thermal stability maintaining 93.8% of
its original value after annealing at 900 C for 2 h
simultaneously.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS
As shown in Figure 1A,B , better performances that
enhance d 33 values, high T C values, and better thermal
stability are simultaneously obtained in CBNLG-C100 x
ceramics, indicating its high potentiality in high temper-
ature applications. The optimum d 33 value of 18.0 pC/N
is achieved in CBNLG-40C ceramic, which is two times
larger than that of the non-doped ceramic (8.6 pC/N), indi-
cating that Ce ion can effectively improve the piezoelectric
properties. The increase of d 33 values may be resulted from
intrinsic and extrinsic factors. For intrinsic aspect, Ce-
doping causes crystal distortion occurring, which changes
crystal symmetry and contributes to the enhancement of
piezoelectric properties. For extrinsic aspect, the domain
structure is closely related to piezoelectric properties.
Comparing CBNLG-0C ceramics with CBNLG-40C ceram-
ics, the size of domains decreases, which is beneficial to an
easy reversal of domains and for further enhancement of

CONCLUSIONS
In summary, Ca 0.86 (LiGd 1 − x Ce x ) 0.07 Bi 2 Nb 2 O 9 (CBNLG-
C100 x , x = 0.0–0.8) ceramics are synthesized by a con-
ventional solid-state reaction method. The structures
and domain structures are investigated of CBNLG-C100 x
ceramics. The crystal structure changes and PFM analysis
show that Ce ion causes smaller and more domains, both
of which play an important role in enhancing piezoelectric
properties. XPS analysis indicates the coexistence of Ce 4 +
and Ce 3 + , and the Raman spectra reveal the possibility of
Ce 4 + replacing Nb 5 + . Therefore, the oxygen vacancy con-
centration increases with the increasing Ce content, lead-
ing to decreased resistivity and enhanced dielectric loss.
The Ca 0.86 (LiGd 0.6 Ce 0.4 ) 0.07 Bi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ceramic shows good
comprehensive performance with high d 33 (18.0 pC/N), T C
( ∼ 930 ◦ C), and ρ dc (1.17 × 10 6 Ω cm at 500 ◦ C). In short,
Ca 0.86 (LiGd 0.6 Ce 0.4 ) 0.07 Bi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ceramic has potential to
apply in high-temperature environment.

text:
Enhanced piezoelectric response of Bi 4 Ti 3 O 12 -based ceramics through
engineered domain configuration and grain size
Wei Shi , Yutong Wu , Hao Tu , Shangyi Guan , Jie Xing , Liang Xu , Hongfei Xu , Qiang Chen
College of Materials Science and Engineering, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Bi Ti O
Grain size effect
Domain configuration
Piezoelectric properties
Dielectric properties
A B S T R A C T
High-temperature ferroelectrics are highly desirable for numerous electromechanical devices such as sensors and
actuators for high-temperature applications. However, it ’ s challenging to achieve high piezoelectricity and T C to
meet the urgent need for high sensitivity and high temperature. Herein, the piezoelectricity of Bi 3.97 Ce 0.03
Ti 2.99 W 0.005 Ta 0.005 O 12 (BCTWT) ceramics is enhanced by engineering domain configuration and grain size. We
have carried out a systematic analysis of the grain size dependent on the electrical performances of BCTWT

have carried out a systematic analysis of the grain size dependent on the electrical performances of BCTWT
ceramics. The d 33 value increases with increasing grain size, a max d 33 value of 36.6 pC/N is obtained at average
grain size of 19.11 µ m. Besides, the reduction of domain size, increasing domain wall (DW) density and weak
pinning effect induce excellent domain switching performances in coarse-grained BCTWT ceramics, which are
mainly responsible for the superior electrical properties. These findings provide a universal approach to
achieving high piezoelectricity of BIT-based ceramics by engineering domain configuration and grain size.
Ferroelectric materials, characterized by spontaneous polarization
( P s ) that can be switched by an external electrical field, are currently
being widely researched for the development of memories, detectors,
transducers and piezoelectric sensors [ 1 ]. Bismuth layer-structured
ferroelectrics (BLSFs) with a representative Aurivillius structure are

transducers and piezoelectric sensors [ 1 ]. Bismuth layer-structured
ferroelectrics (BLSFs) with a representative Aurivillius structure are
becoming one of the promising candidates for high-temperature elec­
tronic devices due to their high Curie temperature ( T C > 500 C) and
excellent temperature stability [ 2 ]. Bismuth titanate (Bi 4 Ti 3 O 12 , BIT), a
member of the BLSFs family, has attracted considerable attention in the
fields of piezoelectricity and catalysis due to its remarkable ferroelectric,
piezoelectric and photocatalytic decomposition performance [ 3 – 7 ]. In
terms of the piezoelectricity of BIT ceramics, a number of studies focus
on the chemical doping strategies and have achieved significant im­
provements. For example, Xie et al. have obtained BIT-based ceramics
with excellent piezoelectricity ( d 33 ~30.5 pC/N) and high-temperature
resistivity ( ρ ~1.24 × 10 Ω⋅ cm at 500 C) by the introduction of
Nb 5 + -Zn 2 + -Nb 5 + ion-pair [ 8 ]. A high piezoelectric coefficient ( d 33 ~31.1

resistivity ( ρ ~1.24 × 10 Ω⋅ cm at 500 C) by the introduction of
Nb 5 + -Zn 2 + -Nb 5 + ion-pair [ 8 ]. A high piezoelectric coefficient ( d 33 ~31.1
pC/N) and large residual polarization ( P = 12.2 μ C/cm ) with a prom­
inent DC resistance ( ρ ~5.49 × 10 Ω⋅ cm at 500 C) have been achieved
in W/Cr doped BIT-based ceramics by Zhang et al. [ 9 ]. Nevertheless, the
microscopic origin of the piezoelectric enhancement of BIT ceramics
remains ambiguous.
In essence, the piezoelectricity of ferroelectrics originates from two
types of contributions, that is, the intrinsic lattice contribution and
extrinsic contribution from the domains [ 10 , 11 ]. However, the contri­
bution from the intrinsic lattice is difficult to verify by experimental
results due to the lack of single crystal as well as the complicated atomic
structure of BIT. Consequently, Tan et al. found that the longitudinal
polarization stretching and in-plane polarization rotation contribute

structure of BIT. Consequently, Tan et al. found that the longitudinal
polarization stretching and in-plane polarization rotation contribute
most to the piezoelectricity of poled polycrystals as studied by
first-principle calculations [ 12 ]. On the other hand, due to the peculiar
crystal structure of BIT, there is a major component of P s lies along the
a -axis [ P s(a) ~50 µ C/cm 2 ] as well as a small component along the c -axis
[ P s(c) ~4 µ C/cm 2 ] [ 13 ]. And these two polarization components, which
can be switched independently of each other, can lead to various types of
domain structures in BIT ceramics [ 14 ]. Using transmission electron
microscopy (TEM), Ye et al. have observed five types of ferroelectric
DWs in Bi 4 Ti 3 O 12 single crystal and revealed the morphology of each
type of domain wall [ 15 ]. Furthermore, some studies have verified that
engineering domain configurations are an effective means to improve
the piezoelectric response of BIT ceramics by piezoresponse force mi­

engineering domain configurations are an effective means to improve
the piezoelectric response of BIT ceramics by piezoresponse force mi­
croscopy (PFM) and TEM [ 16 – 21 ]. However, chemical etching tech­
niques probably provide a more intuitive picture of the configuration
and density of DWs.
Grain size has been verified to have a significant effect on the
ferroelectric,
dielectric,
and
piezoelectric
properties

ferroelectric ceramics [ 22 – 29 ]. There have been few earlier attempts to
study the effect of grain size on the electrical properties of BIT-based
ceramics [ 30 , 31 ]. At the same time, the grain size range of these
studies is limited to a small interval (about 0.25 µ m~5 µ m) and the
dependence of electrical properties is not significant. The reason for the
poor dependency is thought to be related to the control of grain size,
while extremely fine and abnormally grown large grains are difficult to
obtain.
In the present work, superior piezoelectric response of BIT-based
ceramics (Bi 3.97 Ce 0.03 Ti 2.99 W 0.005 Ta 0.005 O 12 , BCTWT) is expected
through engineered domain configuration. Herein, microwave sintering
(MWS) and conventional sintering (CS) were taken to regulate the grain
size of BCTWT. It was found that the electrical properties of BCTWT are
strongly dependent on grain size owing to the different domain config­
urations. Significant improvement in piezoelectric and ferroelectric

strongly dependent on grain size owing to the different domain config­
urations. Significant improvement in piezoelectric and ferroelectric
properties ( d 33 ~36.6 pC/N, P r ~16.4 µ C/cm 2 ) mainly result from the
increased density of P s(a) − 90 DWs and P s(c) − 180 DWs in coarse-
grained (19.11 µ m) BCTWT ceramics. As part of the comprehensive
size effect study, the present work has also investigated the effect of
grain size on the ferroelectric switching and electrical conduction
behavior of BCTWT ceramics.
Powder of composition Bi 3.97 Ce 0.03 Ti 2.99 W 0.005 Ta 0.005 O 12 is pre­
pared by solid-state reaction of raw materials Bi 2 O 3 (99.999 %), TiO 2
(99.99 %), CeO 2 (99.999 %), WO 3 (99.999 %) and Ta 2 O 5 (99.99 %). The
appropriate amount of starting powder is ball-milled in ethanol for 12 h
After drying, the mixture is calcined at 850 C for 4 h and subsequently
the calcined powder is ball-milled again in ethanol for 12 h After drying,

After drying, the mixture is calcined at 850 C for 4 h and subsequently
the calcined powder is ball-milled again in ethanol for 12 h After drying,
the powder is pelletized with 8 % concentration of polyvinyl alcohol
(PVA) and moulded under a uniaxial pressure of 200 MPa. The particles
with coarse-grain are sintered by conventional sintering at 1100 C,
1125 C and 1150 C with a heating rate of 3 C/min for 3 h, while the
particles with fine-grain are obtained by microwave sintering at 1000
C, 1050 C and 1100 C with a heating rate of 50 C/min, holding for 30
min, respectively.
The polished particles are thermally etched at 1050 C for 20 min
and then examined by scanning electron microscopy (S-3400 N, Hitachi,
Japan) detector. Chemical etching essays are carried out with HF/HCl/
H 2 O (volume ratio 1:1:2) and the domain structure of etched surface is
then observed by SEM. Meanwhile, the domain amplitudes and phase
imagines are obtained by PFM (MFP-3D, Asylum Research, Goleta, CA)
scanning.

imagines are obtained by PFM (MFP-3D, Asylum Research, Goleta, CA)
scanning.
The temperature dependence of the dielectric constant ( ε ) and
dielectric loss (tan δ ) are measured by LCR meter (HP4980A, Aligent,
USA) under an ac electric field of 1 V and at 1 MHz. The dc electric re­
sistivity is measured at 10 V within the temperature of 200 C~700 C
with an interval of 25 C by the high resistor (Keithley 6487). The
ferroelectric loops are measured by ferroelectric analyzer (aix-ACCT,
Germany). Poling of pellets is carried out at 200 C for 20 min under a dc
field of 12 kV/mm after coating silver on the surface. The d 33 values of
the polarized samples are performed by a quasi-static d 33 meter (ZJ-6A,
Institute of Acoustics, Academia Sinica, China). And the thermal sta­
bility of d 33 values is determined by thermal depolarization. The
polarized ceramics are kept at different temperatures from room tem­

bility of d 33 values is determined by thermal depolarization. The
polarized ceramics are kept at different temperatures from room tem­
perature to 700 C for 2 h, and their d 33 values are measured at room
temperature.
Scanning electron micrographs of the investigated BCTWT ceramics
sintered under different conditions are shown in Fig. 1 . Fig. 1 (a-c) show
the surface morphology of BCTWT ceramics obtained by MWS. The
grain size of the ceramics is controlled to be small due to the rapid
heating rate and low sintering temperatures of the MWS process. As the
sintering temperature increases of MWS, the matrix grains increase in
grain size and their shapes change to the typical platelike grains of
BLSFs. From the histogram of size distribution shown in the inset of

µ m, 8.40 µ m and 10.41 µ m, respectively. Notably, the CS methods with
high sintering temperatures and prolonged holding times can lead to the
average grain size of ceramics exceeding 14.5 µ m. Furthermore, a few
grains growth abnormally at sintering temperatures higher than 1100 C
according to Fig. 1 (d-f). Their grain lengths even > 100 µ m, and the
average grain size even reaches 19.11 µ m when the sintering tempera­
ture is increased to 1150 C.
The dependence of the piezoelectric coefficient d 33 and thermal
depoling behaviors on the grain size for BCTWT ceramics are shown in

strongly dependent on the grain size. The piezoelectric coefficient of

Abstract
A-site K/Ce and B-site W/Cr co-substituted ­CaBi Nb O ceramics were synthesized by a conventional solid-state reac-
tion process. The structures, piezoelectricity and electrical conduction behaviors were investigated in detail. The
­Ca (K Ce ) Bi Nb (W Cr ) O ceramic exhibited best properties with a high d (piezoelectric coefficient)
of ~ 18.4 pC/N and a high T (Curie temperature) of ~ 917 °C. In addition, the ceramic displayed an excellent thermal stabil-

of ~ 18.4 pC/N and a high T (Curie temperature) of ~ 917 °C. In addition, the ceramic displayed an excellent thermal stabil-
ity performance such that d remained 94% of its initial value even after annealing at 900 °C for 2 h. The planar electro-
mechanical coupling factor was observed to increase from 9.00% at room temperature to 15.24% at 600 °C. Furthermore, a
high electrical resistivity of 1.16 × 10 Ω cm at 600 °C and a good fatigue property were also achieved with this composition.
The ­Ca (K Ce ) Bi Nb (W Cr ) O ceramic was found to be a promising candidate for high-temperature
piezoelectric applications.
1  Introduction
Due to environmental concerns arising from the toxicity of
lead based compounds, there is a need for exploring lead-
free ceramics for piezoelectric applications. Among the
existing lead-free piezoelectric ceramics, Aurivillius phase
ferroelectrics with bismuth-layered perovskite structure
(BLSFs) have received significant attention due to their

existing lead-free piezoelectric ceramics, Aurivillius phase
ferroelectrics with bismuth-layered perovskite structure
(BLSFs) have received significant attention due to their
high Curie temperatures and excellent fatigue properties
[ 1 – 3 ]. This has enabled their applicability in a wide range
of industrial and scientific fields such as high temperature
piezoelectric transducers and nuclear power industries
[ 4 ]. The structure of BLSFs consists of pseudo-perovskite

cations, such as ­Ca , ­Sr , ­Ba , ­K , rare earth ions and so

perovskite layers which can range from 1–6 layers [ 5 , 6 ].
As an important member of the BLSFs, ­CaB Nb O
(CBN) ceramics possesses an ultra-high Curie temperature
( T ) of about 940 °C [ 2 ], making it a potential candidate
for high temperature applications above 600 °C. However,

2  Experimental methods
The ­Ca (K Ce ) Bi Nb (W Cr ) O (CBN-
KCe-WCr) ceramic was prepared using a solid-state reac-
tion technique. ­CaCO (99.99%), ­Bi O (99.99%), ­Nb O
(99.5%), ­K CO (99.5%), ­CeO (99.99%), ­WO (99.8%),
­Cr O (99.95%) were used as raw materials and weighed
according to the stoichiometric compositions. All powders

(99.5%), ­K CO (99.5%), ­CeO (99.99%), ­WO (99.8%),
­Cr O (99.95%) were used as raw materials and weighed
according to the stoichiometric compositions. All powders
were mixed in ethanol in a ball mill for 12 h using a zirconia
grinding media and then the dried mixtures were calcined
at 750 °C for 3 h. The calcined powder was milled again
under the same conditions and pressed into pellets (12 mm in
diameter, 1 mm in thickness) under a pressure of around 200
Mpa using polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) as a binder. After burn-
ing out PVA at 550 °C, the pellets were sintered at 1175 °C
for 3 h. For the electrical measurements, silver paste was
painted on both surfaces of the sintered ceramics and fired
at 825 °C for 20 min in the air atmosphere. The poled disks
were annealed for 2 h from room temperature to 1000 °C and
the d values were measured at room temperature.
The crystalline phases of the samples were determined
by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Ultima IV). The natural surface

4  Conclusions
A modified ultrahigh-temperature piezoelectric ceramic
­Ca (K Ce ) Bi Nb (W Cr ) O was pre-
pared by a conventional solid-state reaction process,
where K/Ce co-substituted the A-site Ca and W/Cr co-
substituted B-site Nb, respectively. The modification by
K/Ce and W/Cr altered the piezoelectric and ferroelectric
properties of CBN ceramic, due to the structural distor-
tion, microstructure optimization and reduction of oxygen
vacancy concentration. A high d value of 18.4 pC/N,
high T of 917 °C, high remanent polarization of 11.88
μC/cm and a large field-induced strain of 0.018% were
observed in CBN-KCe-WCr ceramic. Additionally, an

high T of 917 °C, high remanent polarization of 11.88
μC/cm and a large field-induced strain of 0.018% were
observed in CBN-KCe-WCr ceramic. Additionally, an
excellent thermal stability of 17.3 pC/N was also obtained
in the ceramic, which persisted even after annealing at
900 °C. This work demonstrates that A-site and B-site
co-modification can lead to better piezoelectric properties
as compared to individual A-site or B-site modifications
and the CBN-KCe-WCr ceramic can be suitable for high-
temperature piezoelectric applications.

IV. DISCUSSION
The lower piezoactivity for y =0.7 and 0.8 compared
with y =0.5 can be explained by the far greater range of x
over which rhombohedral and tetragonal phases coexist for
higher Fe concentrations. For y =0.5, the narrow range of x
 2–3 mol %  represents a classical MPB similar to PZT in
which the rhombohedral and tetragonal phases are close in
free energy within the majority of the ceramic. Consequently,
the extrinsic contribution by domain wall motion to the pi-
ezoactivity is maximized. In the case of y =0.7 and 0.8, a
pseudo- rather than classical-MPB is observed in the solid
solution within which rhombohedral and tetragonal phases
coexist. Therefore, for any given composition within the
pseudo-MPB, only a small volume fraction contains rhom-
bohedral and tetragonal phases of similar free energy and
switching between the  001  and  111  polarization vectors

of the heterogeneity at y   0.5 may be either kinetic or ther-

1. Introduction
With the development of aircraft, aerospace and nuclear power in­
dustries, the demand for high-temperature ( > 600 C) piezoelectric de­
vices has dramatically increased, such as accelerometers and sensors
used to detect and record dynamic mechanical parameters at harsh
conditions [ 1 – 3 ]. Considering the usage temperature upper limit of lead
zirconate titanate (PZT) is only about 320 – 430 C [ 3 ], it is urgently
needed to find alternatives that can be used in much higher temperature
range. Bismuth-layered structure ferroelectrics (BLSFs) with formula of
(Bi 2 O 2 ) 2 þ (A m-1 B m O 3m þ 1 ) 2- have attracted great attention because of the

range. Bismuth-layered structure ferroelectrics (BLSFs) with formula of
(Bi 2 O 2 ) 2 þ (A m-1 B m O 3m þ 1 ) 2- have attracted great attention because of the
high Curie temperature [ 4 , 5 ]. Among them, CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 is considered to
be a particularly important member with remarkable Curie temperature
of 940 C, which might be used in high temperature environment
beyond 600 C [ 6 ]. However, the d 33 value of pristine CBN ceramic is
low (~5 pC/N), which greatly limits its practical application [ 7 ].
Several approaches have been developed to promote the piezoelec­
tric properties of CBN-based ceramics [ 8 – 14 ]. Thereinto A-site doping is
considered as a valid approach to tailor the crystalline structure of CBN,
which could effectively improve the piezoelectric activity. Previously,
d 33 values of 13.3, 16, 16 pC/N have been reported in Li/Ce, Na/Ce,
K/Ce co-modified CBN ceramics [ 8 – 10 ]. Furthermore, several studies
also revealed that suitable A-site triatomic doping could effectively

K/Ce co-modified CBN ceramics [ 8 – 10 ]. Furthermore, several studies
also revealed that suitable A-site triatomic doping could effectively
tailor the pseudo-morphotropic phase boundary, which was helpful to
improve the piezoelectric properties of CBN-based ceramics. With A-site
(X, Li, Ce) doping, CBN-based ceramics showed better d 33 of 13.1and
15.3 pC/N (X ¼ Nd and Bi, respectively) [ 11 , 12 ]. Moreover, Liu et al.
recently found that A-site Li/Bi doping and (Bi 2 O 2 ) 2 þ layers Ce doping in
CBN ceramic can manipulate the pseudo-morphotropic phase boundary.
A remarkable piezoelectric constant of (20.2 pC/N) and a good thermal
depoling performance ( d 33 remained 89.6% of its initial value after
depoling at 875 C) were achieved [ 13 ]. Unfortunately, only a few
successful attempts on B-site modification of CBN ceramics were re­
ported, which might be ascribed to the fact that most of the cations that
could enter the B-site have similar sizes and may not play a major

could enter the B-site have similar sizes and may not play a major

Recently, B-site co-doping strategy with mixed-valence cations was
developed to enhance the piezoelectric properties of some BLSF ce­

~38 pC/N in B-site Nb/Cu co-doped Bi 4 Ti 3 O 12 ceramics, which was the

4. Conclusions
Mixed valence cations Mo/Cr modified CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ceramics were
prepared using the conventional solid-state sintering method. Mo/Cr co-
doped in B site reduced oxygen vacancies remarkably and enhanced the
tetragonality of lattice structure, thus improved the piezoelectric prop­
erties, thermal stability and resistivity of the ceramics. Especially, the
ceramic with a composition of x ¼ 0.07 exhibited an optimized piezo­
electricity with a high d 33 of ~15 pC/N and an ultra-high T C of ~939 C.

ceramic with a composition of x ¼ 0.07 exhibited an optimized piezo­
electricity with a high d 33 of ~15 pC/N and an ultra-high T C of ~939 C.
Moreover, an excellent thermal stability performance that d 33 remained
93% of its original value even after being annealed at 850 C for 2 h and
an excellent electrical resistivity of 3.33  10 5 Ω  cm at 600 C were also
achieved in this ceramic. This study further proved that B-site mixed
valence cations co-doping can be employed to tailor piezoelectric
properties of BLSFs, in addition to manipulating the phase boundary.

ABSTRACT
A synergetic effect of Li/Nd at the A site and W/Mn at the B site co-substitution on electrical properties of calcium bismuth niobate
(CaBi Nb O , CBNO)-based ceramics is proposed in this paper. CBNO primarily shows mixed p -type and ionic conduction due to a trace of
oxygen vacancies (V
). Both bulk resistivity ( q ) and activity energy ( E ) for conduction are dramatically increased by the co-substitution in

concentration. Furthermore, the synergetic effect of Li/Nd at the

is a good promising material in high-temperature piezoelectric applications.

received increasing attention due to their potential applications in the
ﬁelds of aerospace, automotive, power plants, and material processing.
To date, single crystal of quartz (SiO ) is still the main commercially

To date, single crystal of quartz (SiO ) is still the main commercially
high-temperature piezoelectric material. The shortcomings of quartz are
relatively low piezoelectric coefﬁcient ( d  2 pC/N) and low working

T (  1000–1400 C) and comparable d (  4–7 pC/N).

1. Introduction
In recent years, the aerospace, aircraft, and nuclear power industries
have a desperate need for sensors, which can operate at 500 °C or
higher temperature with a long mean time between failures, because
sensors need to be as close as possible to engine component of interest
for adequate sensitivity to monitor engine health and enable safer op-
eration [1,2] . Aurivillius phase compounds, called as bismuth layered
structural ferroelectrics (BLSFs), are a large family of important and
interesting ferroelectrics, possessing some unique properties such as
high Curie temperature and fatigue-free properties. These shining
properties make Aurivillius compounds as promising candidates for
high-temperature piezoelectric sensors operating in some hazardous
environments [1 – 4] . Therefore, these compounds have attracted in-
creasing attention in recent years. The structure of these compounds

2. Experimental
Aurivillius type Ca (Li Ce Nd ) Bi Nb O (CBNLBN-100 x ,
where x = 0, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2 and 0.25) ceramics were
prepared by a conventional solid-state reaction route. Metal oxides,
Bi O (99%), CaCO (99%), Nb O (99.5%), Li CO (98%), CeO
(99.9%), and Nd O (99.9%) were used as raw materials. All powders
were weighed according to stoichiometric compositions and then mixed
by ball milling in ethanol for 6 h with ZrO balls as milling media. The
slurry was dried at 70 °C to remove ethanol and then calcined at 850 °C
for 2 h. Calcined powders were milled again under the same conditions
and granulated with polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) as a binder. The powders
were ﬁ nally pressed into disks of ~ 10 mm in diameter and ~ 1 mm
thickness in a steel die at a pressure of ∼ 5 T . After burning out the

were ﬁ nally pressed into disks of ~ 10 mm in diameter and ~ 1 mm
thickness in a steel die at a pressure of ∼ 5 T . After burning out the
binder at 550 °C, the green pellets were sintered at 1050 °C for 2 h.
The crystal structure of the sintered ceramics was determined using
an X-ray di ﬀ ractometer (X ′ Pert PRO, PANalytical, Holland) equipped
with Cu-K α radiation ( λ = 1.5418 Å). The microstructure of the sin-
tered ceramics was characterized by scanning electron microscopy
(SEM, S4800, Hitachi, Japan). Both the surfaces of the sintered cera-
mics were ground and polished into ~ 0.5-mm thick disk, and then ﬁ red
Ag/Pd paste at 850 °C for 10 min as the electrodes. The dielectric be-
havior as a function of temperature was investigated using an LCR
analyzer (IM3536, Hioki, Japan) attached to a programmable furnace.
The temperature dependence of the electrical conductivity was mea-
sured over the temperature range from 300 to 700 °C at a heating rate

The temperature dependence of the electrical conductivity was mea-
sured over the temperature range from 300 to 700 °C at a heating rate
of 5 °C/min. The specimens were poled in a silicone oil bath at 180 °C
under a DC electric ﬁ eld of 5 – 12 kV/mm for 5 – 15 min. The piezo-
electric coe ﬃ cient d was measured using a quasi-static d meter (ZJ-

4. Conclusions
In summary, Aurivillius phase structural CaBi Nb O ceramics with
(Li, Ce, Nd) multi-dopants were successfully prepared by the conven-
tional solid-state sintering method. XRD patterns of all compounds
exhibited single phase structure, and no secondary phase was detected.
There should be two types of physical mechanism in the variation of a /
b . At the beginning, (Li, Ce, Nd) multi-dopants with smaller size in A
site increased orthorhombic distortion. However, with increasing do-
pants, A-site Bi ions were replaced by the dopants gradually, de-
creasing the orthorhombic distortion and leading to a tendency from
orthorhombic system to tetragonal system in the crystal structure. The
piezoelectric coe ﬃ cient d value was signi ﬁ cantly increased by the
substitution of (Li, Ce, Nd). CBNLCN-15 ceramics possessed optimal
piezoelectric properties ( d ~ 13.1 pC/N, T > 900 °C), which would
be attributed to decreasing grain sizes and morphotropic phase

substitution of (Li, Ce, Nd). CBNLCN-15 ceramics possessed optimal
piezoelectric properties ( d ~ 13.1 pC/N, T > 900 °C), which would
be attributed to decreasing grain sizes and morphotropic phase
boundary (MPB). In addition, the piezoelectric properties of CBNLCN-
15 ceramics exhibit excellent thermal stability that remained 86% of
their initial d values (13.1 pC/N) after annealing at 850 °C for 2 h.

A B S T R A C T
Calcium bismuth niobate (CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ) is regarded as one of the most potential high-temperature piezoelectric
materials owing to its highest Curie point in bismuth layer-structured ferroelectrics. Nevertheless, low piezo-
electric coef ﬁ cient and low resistivity at high temperature considerably restrict its development as key electronic

electric coef ﬁ cient and low resistivity at high temperature considerably restrict its development as key electronic
components. Herein, markedly improved piezoelectric properties and DC resistivity of CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ceramics
through Na þ and Sm 3 þ co-doping are reported. The nominal compositions Ca 1-2 x (Na, Sm) x Bi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ( x ¼ 0, 0.01,
0.025, and 0.05) ceramics have been prepared via the conventional solid state method. An optimum composition
of Ca 0.95 (Na, Sm) 0.025 Bi 2 Nb 2 O 9 is obtained, which possesses a high Curie point of ~949 C, a piezoelectric co-
ef ﬁ cient of ~12.8 pC/N, and a DC electrical resistivity at 500 C of ~4  10 7 Ω ⋅ cm. The improved d 33 is probably
ascribed to the reduction in domain size and the increase in domain wall density caused by the reduced grain size.
More importantly, after annealing at 900 C for 2 h, the piezoelectric coef ﬁ cient still maintains about 90% of the

More importantly, after annealing at 900 C for 2 h, the piezoelectric coef ﬁ cient still maintains about 90% of the
initial d 33 value, which displays a signi ﬁ cant improvement compared to pure CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ceramic with only 44%
of the initial d 33 value. This work exhibits a feasible approach to simultaneously obtain high piezoelectric
property and thermal stability in CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ceramics by Na þ /Sm 3 þ co-doping.

The donor-acceptor co-doping strategy was reported to be a simple
and effective way to signi ﬁ cantly improve the piezoelectric coef ﬁ cient
and its thermal stability, which is powerfully demonstrated in BaTiO 3
(BT) system [ 10 – 12 ]. In BT system, not only the improvement of piezo-

effects: ﬁ rst, the lattice distortion caused by the difference in ion radii
between doped ions and original ions is bene ﬁ cial to the improvement of
piezoelectric properties; second, defect dipoles caused by the ion pairs
are also favorable to the improvement of the piezoelectric properties and
its thermal stability [ 10 , 11 ]. Considering the existence of similar
perovskite layers in BLSFs, this co-doping strategy has also been

having a positive effect on the piezoelectric properties [ 23 , 42 ].
In previous study, Sm 3 þ has been utilized to modify CBN, however,
dissatisfactory result ( d 33 is only 11.5 pC/N) was obtained [ 31 ]. In this
article, Na þ /Sm 3 þ ion pairs, in which Na þ acts as the acceptor dopant
while Sm 3 þ acts as the donor dopant, were exploited to modify CBN to
obtain a better piezoelectric property and thermal stability. Better

obtained in Na þ /Sm 3 þ co-doped CBN ceramics. The effect of Na þ /Sm 3 þ
co-doping on microstructure, defects as well as electrical properties was
systematically investigated.

3. Conclusion
CBNNS- x ceramics were prepared by the conventional solid-state
method, and the phase structure, microscopic morphology, and elec-
trical properties were systematically characterized. All samples were

method, and the phase structure, microscopic morphology, and elec-
trical properties were systematically characterized. All samples were
single phase and their grain morphology showed a typical ﬂ at-plate
structure. And striped domains and layered structure are clearly
observed respectively in overview bright ﬁ eld image and HRTEM image.
The Na þ /Sm 3 þ doping reduced the orthorhombicity of CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ce-
ramics, and the piezoelectric properties of the doped CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9
ceramics are signi ﬁ cantly enhanced, which was attributed to the further
separation of the positive and negative charge centers due to the
increased degree of distortion and the high resistivity allowing them to
be poled under higher electric ﬁ elds. In addition, thermal depolarization
performance tests showed that the piezoelectric coef ﬁ cient d 33 of
CBNNS-0.025 ceramics remained close to 90% after annealing at 900 C.

4. Experimental
The compositions of Ca 1- x (Na, Sm) x Bi 2 Nb 2 O 9 abbreviated as CBNNS-
x ( x ¼ 0, 0.01, 0.025, and 0.05)) ceramics were fabricated via the con-
ventional solid state method. CaCO 3 (99.9%), Na 2 CO 3 (99.9%), Sm 2 O 3
(99.99%), Bi 2 O 3 (99.9%) and Nb 2 O 5 (99.9%) were utilized as raw ma-
terials to synthesize the above-mentioned compounds. The raw materials
were weighed in accordance with the stoichiometric ratio, and then
mixed by ball milling for 8 h using anhydrous ethanol as solvent and
zirconia balls with different size ratios as the milling medium. After being
dried, these mixtures were calcined at 925 C for 2 h. After this, powders
after being calcined were re-milled for 24 h in the same condition, which

dried, these mixtures were calcined at 925 C for 2 h. After this, powders
after being calcined were re-milled for 24 h in the same condition, which
were mixed using 5 wt % polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) aqueous solution as a

The phase structure of CBNNS- x ceramics was examined by an X-ray
diffraction meter (XRD, Advance D8, Bruker, Switzerland) using Cu K α
radiation ( λ ¼ 0.15406 nm). The grain morphology of CBNNS- x ceramics
was observed by ﬁ eld-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM,
Nova Nano SEM230, FEI Electron Optics B.V, Czech Republic). The
densities of CBNNS- x ceramics were measured using the Archimedes
method. The P - E and I - E hysteresis loops were measured using ferro-
electric tester (aixACCT Analyzer TF3000). A transmission electron mi-
croscope (Titan G2 60 – 300, FEI, USA) was used to obtain transmission
electron microscopy (TEM) and high-resolution transmission electron

croscope (Titan G2 60 – 300, FEI, USA) was used to obtain transmission
electron microscopy (TEM) and high-resolution transmission electron
microscopy (HRTEM) images, as well as selected area electron diffraction
(SAED) patterns. For TEM characterization, samples were processed by
focused ion beam (FIB) milling (Helios Nanolab G3 UC, FEI, USA).
Chemical composition and the valence states of the elements were
analyzed via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCALAB250Xi,
Thermo Fisher Scienti ﬁ c, USA). Temperature-dependent permittivity and
dielectric loss were measured by using a dielectric measurement system
(TZDM, RT-1000) connected to a programmed furnace with a step of 5
C/min. The room temperature frequency-dependent dielectric perfor-
mance of CBNNS- x ceramics poled in different poling electric ﬁ elds was
measured using an LCR meter (Agilent 4294A). Variable-temperature
direct-current (DC) resistance of CBNNS- x ceramics was measured

measured using an LCR meter (Agilent 4294A). Variable-temperature
direct-current (DC) resistance of CBNNS- x ceramics was measured
using a resistivity tester with a test voltage of 100 V (RMS-1000P, Par-
tulab, China). Sintered ceramics were poled in silicone oil at 200 C
under different DC electric ﬁ eld (200 – 250 kV/cm) for about 30 – 60 min.
The piezoelectric coef ﬁ cient d 33 of samples which were poled by direct
current ﬁ eld was measured at room temperature by using a quasi-static
piezometer (ZJ-6, Institute of Acoustics, Chinese Academic of Science,
Beijing, China). For evaluating thermal stability, thermal depolarization
experiments were implemented by heating the poled samples from room
temperature to selected temperatures and holding them at the selected
temperature for 2 h and then naturally cooling to room temperature to
measure d 33 . This procedure was repeated many times from room tem-
perature to Curie point.

(K, Na)NbO -Based Lead-Free Piezoceramics: Fundamental Aspects,
Processing Technologies, and Remaining Challenges
Jing-Feng Li,* Ke Wang, Fang-Yuan Zhu, Li-Qian Cheng, and Fang-Zhou Yao
State Key Laboratory of New Ceramics and Fine Processing, School of Materials Science and Engineering,
Tsinghua University, 100084 Beijing, China
Environment-friendly lead-free piezoelectric ceramics have been
studied extensively in the past decade with great progress
particularly in systems based on a niobate perovskite com-
pound formulated as (K, Na)NbO (abbreviated as KNN). A
comprehensive review on the latest development of KNN-based
piezoelectric ceramics is presented in this article, including the
phase structure, property enhancement approaches, and sinter-
ing processes as well as the status of some promising applica-
tions. The phase structure of KNN was reexamined and
associated with the eﬀect of chemical modiﬁcation on its
tetragonal-to-orthorhombic transition. Then, a special focus is

mechanical load was ﬁrst discovered by the Curie brothers in
1880, whereas the eﬀect that links a mechanical action
(stress or strain) with an electric response (electric ﬁeld, dis-
placement, or polarization) is named the piezoelectric eﬀect
or, more precisely, the direct piezoelectric eﬀect. Later, it was
experimentally
conﬁrmed
that
the
converse
piezoelectric
eﬀect is also observed in single crystals with acentric symme-

or, more precisely, the direct piezoelectric eﬀect. Later, it was
experimentally
conﬁrmed
that
the
converse
piezoelectric
eﬀect is also observed in single crystals with acentric symme-
try in that an external electric ﬁeld generates a mechanical
response, i.e., a stress or strain of the sample, similar to the
electrostriction of dielectrics. It is generally recognized that
the intrinsic piezoelectric eﬀect reﬂects a linear relationship
between electrical and mechanical variables and originates
from the displacement of ions of a single crystal with acentric
symmetry under an applied electric ﬁeld. This relationship
enables a change in the sign of the eﬀect by switching the
external electric ﬁeld, unlike the electrostriction that always
exhibits a quadratic expansion.
Although piezoelectricity is found in several types of natu-
ral materials, most modern devices use polycrystalline ceram-
ics, which can be easily fabricated and shaped at low cost.

II.
Phase Structure
It is surprising that K Na NbO ceramics were investi-
gated intensively several decades ago both in material prop-
erties and structures, as it was found as a piezoelectric
material in as early as 1950s. Although KNbO and NaN-
bO can form solid solutions with a perovskite structure
regardless of x value, as shown in Fig. 2, they have distinct
symmetries. Generally, pure KNbO has the following poly-
