dral (R) phase, room-temperature orthorhombic (O) phase,
and high-temperature tetragonal (T, 225 ° C ~ 435 ° C) and
cubic (C, > 435 ° C) phase. In contrast, phase transitions of
NaNbO are more complicated that there are as many as
seven polymorphs across the whole temperature range. The
room-temperature polymorph of NaNbO was reported to
be orthorhombic and antiferroelectric, with the space group
Pbma . The complexity of the structure of NaNbO is
strengthened by an oxygen octahedral tilting, which is absent
in KNbO . This could be possibly due to the fact that K is
relatively large enough to ﬁll the 12-coordinated cavity of the
ideal perovskite structure. It is interesting to note that only

III.
Property Enhancement
In general, the piezoelectric output in ferroelectric ceramics is
composed of intrinsic and extrinsic contributions. The former
refers to linear piezoelectric eﬀect of lattice displacement,
whereas the latter originates mainly from movement of
domain walls. As derived from the Landau – Devonshire –
Ginzburg phenomenological relation, the linear piezoelectric
eﬀect is proportional to the magnitude of P ; therefore, the
larger P , the higher the piezoelectric coeﬃcient is expected.
Typical P values of KNN-based materials are in the range
from 15 to 25 l C/cm , comparable to those of PZT types.
One may suggest that the discrepancy in the piezoelectric
properties between KNN and PZT could be largely due to

text:
from 15 to 25 l C/cm , comparable to those of PZT types.
One may suggest that the discrepancy in the piezoelectric
properties between KNN and PZT could be largely due to
the diﬀerence in the extrinsic contribution. However, it is
considered by the authors that clear distinguishment between
these two contributions may be impractical. For example,
the enhancement in dielectric, piezoelectric, and electrome-
chanical coupling properties along the MPB in PZT-based
ceramics is normally attributed to facilitated polarization
switching, which holds true even for monodomain single
crystals, indicating the intrinsic nature of MPB. How-
ever, it is, of course, undeniable that facilitated domain wall
movement in the MPB region would further beneﬁt the pie-
zoelectric performances. In any case, we can conclude that
the control over the phase structure is important for piezoce-
ramics; particularly creating a two-phase coexisting state is
preferred, which can be either due to compositionally driven

ramics; particularly creating a two-phase coexisting state is
preferred, which can be either due to compositionally driven
MPB or temperature-driven PPT eﬀect. The manipulation of
phase structures in KNN is usually realized via composi-
tional modiﬁcation, which is the ﬁrst topic in this part. In
addition, alternative is a domain engineering, which can
enhance piezoelectric performances in KNN-based ceramics.
In the last part of the present section, we review the issues
concerning temperature instability arising from the PPT
eﬀect and discuss possible solutions.
(1)
Chemical Modiﬁcation
As aforementioned, KNN ceramics by conventional sintering
is reported with a moderate piezoelectric constant d around
80 pC/N half a century ago, which was improved to
~ 125 pC/N recently. If the K/Na ratio is elaborately
optimized, higher d even up to 160 pC/N can also be
achieved. It should be noted that the d could be improved

optimized, higher d even up to 160 pC/N can also be
achieved. It should be noted that the d could be improved
to 150 ~ 160 pC/N using pressure-assisted techniques such as
hot pressing (HP) and spark plasma sintering (SPS), without
intentional optimization of K/Na ratio. Not many
reports concerning chemical modiﬁcation in this system come
out until the year 2004, when a breakthrough was made
by Saito et al. that a signiﬁcantly high d over 400 pC/N
was realized in KNN by multiple dopants of Li, Ta, and Sb,
as well as well-controlled texturing technique. Actually, it is
considered that this discovery has opened up a seeming cam-

improvement of piezoelectric constant d , which is usually
measured using the convenient quasi-static method (Berlin-

it was proposed that the underlying mechanism for property
enhancement of KNN-based ceramics by means of these

ceramics has been a subject of recent studies, most
of which point out that poling temperature is of signiﬁcant
importance, with respect to individual compositions as well

be utilized to manipulate interior dipole movement, which

IV.
Sintering of KNN-Based Ceramics
(1)
Normal Sintering
It is known that KNN ceramics have been accepted as one
of the promising lead-free materials since 1950s. How-
ever, at ﬁrst it was a big challenge to obtain highly dense
bulk
samples
by
normal
sintering.
Later
in
1962,
an
advanced fabrication technique of HP was introduced by
Jaeger and Egerton, resulting in high bulk density ( ~ 95% of
theoretical density) with enhanced properties, e.g., high Curie
temperature ( T ~ 420 ° C), large d ( ~ 160 pC/N) and k
( ~ 45%). Nevertheless, normal sintering has still been pre-
ferred in the community due to its signiﬁcant advantages in
shaping ﬂexibility and cost eﬃciency. It should be noted that
the sintering temperature of KNN-based ceramics is rela-
tively high (over 1000 ° C), considering its melting point at

crystallographic planes with the lowest surface energy.

Generally, the sintering temperature of KNN is relatively
high near its melting point, resulting in ineluctable appear-
ance of liquid phase. As a consequence, possibility of solid-
state sintering is signiﬁcantly reduced.
Appearance of liquid phase during sintering promotes the
AGG behavior as well as secondary phase. Gener-
ally, grain growth is classiﬁed into two types: normal and
abnormal
(exaggerated)
grain
growth.
Normal
grain
growth is characterized by unimodal distribution of relative
grain sizes with time; in contrast, AGG involves some unex-
pectedly large grains out of a matrix of ﬁne grains, showing
a bimodal grain size distribution. Here, the grain growth
behavior of KNN will be addressed in terms of the micro-
structure changes as a function of sintering temperatures.

tures, the microstructure evolution is similar to a grain
coalescence process [Fig. 12(a)]. First, a homogeneous micro-

For the KNN-based ceramics sintered at elevated tempera-

coalescence process [Fig. 12(a)]. First, a homogeneous micro-
structure with quadrate grain shape powders ( ~ 500 nm to
~ 1 l m) shows up at relatively low sintering temperature.
Then when the sintering temperature passes through a criti-
cal point, the grain coalescence suddenly appears in certain
part of grains, which exaggerated to 2 – 5 l m in size, as
shown in Figs. 12(b) – (d); meanwhile, other grains still retain
their original shapes and sizes. When the sintering tempera-
ture further increases, the liquid phase may be formed which
accelerates the particle redistribution because of the enhanced
diﬀusion process.

(2)
Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS)
To achieve much enhanced piezo/ferroelectric properties,
special sintering techniques are required, such as HP and
SPS. In principle, SPS is similar to HP, although it has its
unique features, e.g., low sintering temperatures, stress-
assisted densiﬁcation process, large current shock eﬀect, etc.
Although it is still argued whether the plasma is truly
involved during sintering or not, SPS has been successfully
employed
to
manufacture
high-performance
KNN-based
ceramics.
It is generally considered that SPS is an ideal tool for
sintering KNN-like ceramics, which is highly volatile while
diﬃcult to be sintered at solid state. The SPS apparatus gen-
erally consists of a uniaxial pressing system, in which water-
cooled punches serve as electrodes. The powders are placed
inside a graphite die and then the chamber is evacuated

cooled punches serve as electrodes. The powders are placed
inside a graphite die and then the chamber is evacuated
before sintering. After power on, the pulsed DC generator,
which supplies a huge current up to 1000 A and enormously
enhanced heating speed, will work together with complicated
pressure-, position-, and temperature- controlling systems.
This technique utilizes a synergic eﬀect between a consider-
ably high pressure (20 – 100 MPa) and fast heating rate
(100 ° C/min – 300 ° C/min), realizing highly dense bulk ceramics
with ﬁne grains within several minutes. For
example, pure KNN ceramics have been successfully sintered
at a temperature as low as 920 ° C, which is about 200 ° C
lower than that for normal sintering. Up to ~ 99% of density
was achieved with an enhanced d up to 148 pC/N. It is
noticed that normal sintering usually results in 92% of den-

the SPS technique, which turns out successful in most cases

The aforementioned examples indicate that it is possible to

KNN is not necessarily required to substitute all the PZT
family as an “all-round player,” while it does provide com-
petitive performances against at least certain types of PZT,

“hard”
PZT
(a
typical

is
PZT-8;

the vast applications of these speciﬁc PZT types, environ-
mental issues could be improved step by step, where KNN-
based piezoceramics play an important role. On the other

(1)
KNN-Based 1 – 3 Composite
Generally, KNN possesses lower permittivity e as well as
mechanical quality factor Q , when compared with PZT ceram-
ics. Nevertheless, these features could be favorable for trans-
ducer-oriented applications, such as ultrasonic imaging.
Assuming a given composition of piezoceramics, the coupling
factor for these kinds of applications can be further enhanced if
the material forms 1 – 3-type composite together with polymers.
The 1 – 3 piezoceramic/polymer composites are applied espe-
cially for high-frequency hydrophones and biomedical imaging
transducers. Normally, two component parts are

text:
is possible to attain high piezoelectric coeﬃcient d over
400 pC/N even in nontextured KNN ceramics by elaborated
chemical modiﬁcations, although there still remain some crit-
ical challenges for large-scale applications.
At ﬁrst, creating a real MPB as in PZT system should be
a breakthrough to resolve the relatively large temperature
dependence of piezoelectric properties of KNN-based ceram-
ics, which is full of scientiﬁc interest and technical impor-
tance. For this, more studies about the phase structure and
phase diagram of KNN system are indispensable. Another
challenge for KNN-based ceramics is that alkali elements at
A-site in KNN are easy to evaporate during sintering pro-
cess. Given that the A-site chemical composition is critical to
the phase control and hence property enhancement in the
KNN-based ceramics, more innovative processing techniques
should be continuously developed. Eventually, processing
techniques should be well established to guarantee reliable
mass production at an industry scale.

should be continuously developed. Eventually, processing
techniques should be well established to guarantee reliable
mass production at an industry scale.
Finally, there have been some prototypical applications
using KNN-based ceramics even in industry, which are
important and encouraging for the community to push the
lead-free piezoelectric research forward. We believe that lead-
free piezoelectric nanomaterials will also ﬁnd more applica-
tions with the advancement of micro- and nanotechnologies
for energy harvesting and medical diagnostic devices. Of
course, whether lead-free piezoelectric ceramics can be uti-
lized in a large scale depends greatly on the governmental
regulations on the PZT-based piezoceramics. Apart from
this, more and more fundamental and practical studies for
developing higher performance lead-free piezoelectric ceram-
ics with well-balanced electrical properties and wide process-
ing tolerance will be the key to success for the ﬁeld.

A B S T R A C T
Nb – Mg co-doped CaBi Ti O ceramics were synthesized for potential high temperature piezoelectric applica-
tions via the solid-state reaction technique. The in ﬂ uences of Nb – Mg doping level on structure, piezoelectricity
and other electrical properties were systematically researched. The XRD, EDS and Raman scattering results
con ﬁ rmed that the doped Nb – Mg ions had successfully di ﬀ used into the crystal lattice of CaBi Ti O ceramic.
Co-doping of Nb – Mg enhanced the piezoelectric coe ﬃ cient d e ﬀ ectively without causing signi ﬁ cant dete-
rioration on Curie temperature T . The CaBi Ti (Nb Mg ) O ceramic possessed the optimized electric
properties with a high d value of 24 pC/N accompanied by a high T value of 787 °C. In addition, this ceramic
also exhibited a good thermal stability with d keeping 91% of its original value after annealing at 600 °C. All

also exhibited a good thermal stability with d keeping 91% of its original value after annealing at 600 °C. All
these results suggested that Nb – Mg co-doped CaBi Ti O ceramic could be a potential candidate for high
temperature piezoelectric sensor or detector applications.
1. Introduction
In recent years, there are growing demands for sensors that can be
applied at high temperature, such as electric fuel injection piezoelectric
valve for internal combustion, ultrasonic locator in nuclear reactor, etc .
[ 1 , 2 ]. Hence, it is urgently needed to explore piezoelectric ceramics
which has good piezoelectric properties with high Curie temperature
and excellent thermal stabilities. Bismuth layer-structured ferroelectrics
(BLSFs) ceramics have been considered as ideal candidates and caught
great attention from both academics and industries. It is not only be-
cause their ultra-high Curie temperature (approximately 600 – 900 °C),
but also the lead-free and low manufacturing cost [ 3 , 4 ].

cause their ultra-high Curie temperature (approximately 600 – 900 °C),
but also the lead-free and low manufacturing cost [ 3 , 4 ].
The general formula of BLSFs is the (Bi O ) (A B O ) , of
which (Bi O ) is ﬂ uorite-like layer along the c axis, and unit of (A
B O ) is pseudo-perovskite structure [ 5 , 6 ]. In formula, A is a
mono-, di-, trivalent ions (such as Na , Ca ,Sr , La and Bi ,
etc. ), or combination of them, as well as B is a tetravalent, pentavalent
and hexavalent transition element ( e.g. , Fe , Cr , Ti , Nb , Ta ,
W , Mo ) [ 7 ]. The range of (BO ) octahedra m usually belongs to
1 – 6. CaBi Ti O (CBT) is a typical Aurivillius structure ferroelectrics
with m = 4, which A-site is consisted of Ca and Bi ions while B-site
is occupied by Ti . It was reported that pristine CBT had a rather high
Curie point ( T = 790 °C) and a low dielectric loss (tan δ = 0.2%),
which made it as one of the most noteworthy high temperature pie-
zoelectric materials [ 5 , 8 ]. However, the piezoelectric coe ﬃ cient value

which made it as one of the most noteworthy high temperature pie-
zoelectric materials [ 5 , 8 ]. However, the piezoelectric coe ﬃ cient value
( d = 7 pC/N) is extremely low because the switching of spontaneous
polarization is limited to the a-b plane. Additionally, CBT possesses a
low resistivity ( ρ ) and a large coercive ﬁ eld ( E ).
To improve the electrical properties of CBT-based ceramics, it would
be a feasible approach to substitute isovalent or heterovalent ions for
Ca . Yan et al. obtained a high d value of 17 pC/N in CBT ceramic by
Na and Ce doping at Ca-site [ 9 ]. Similar enhancements of d value
were also achieved in K/Ce and Li/Ce doped CBT ceramics [ 10 ]. In
addition, Sheng et al. recently obtained a CBT-based ceramics with a
remarkable d value of 19 pC/N by introducing double rare earth ions
Nd and Ce at Bi-site, which indicates that substitution of Bi ions

piezoelectric activities of CBT ceramic [ 11 ]. Nevertheless, the piezo-
electric activities of ceramics reported by above literatures via double
ions doping at Bi-site or Ca-site are still relatively low until now. In
addition, the improvement of piezoelectricity of CBT ceramic by co-
doping at Ca-site or Bi-site is usually accompanied by a deterioration of
thermal stability, which greatly a ﬀ ects its practical applications at high
temperature. Therefore, studies are still needed to fabricate CBT-based
ceramics which have enhanced piezoelectric properties with optimized
thermal stabilities.
In the past several decades, co-doping with mixed-valence ions at
Ti-site is reported to be e ﬀ ective in strengthening piezoelectricity of the
PZT system [ 12 , 13 ]. Some researchers recently had introduced this co-
doping strategy into the modi ﬁ cation of BLSFs. For example, Long et al.

PZT system [ 12 , 13 ]. Some researchers recently had introduced this co-
doping strategy into the modi ﬁ cation of BLSFs. For example, Long et al.
fabricated Nb – Mg co-doped Bi Ti O ceramics with an excellent d
value of 30 pC/N [ 14 ]. Li et al. prepared Nb – Cu co-doped the Bi Ti O
ceramics, and then achieved an increased d value of 38 pC/N [ 15 ].
Moreover, a remarkable d value of 15 pC/N was recently acquired in
W/Cr co-doped CaBi Nb O ceramics. All these work demonstrated the
great potentials of co-doping with mixed-valence ions at Ti-site in im-
proving the piezoelectric properties of BLSFs. Especially, Shen et al.
recently introduced Nb and Mn ions to the Ti-site of CaBi Ti O
ceramics and an increased d value ~23 pC/N was obtained [ 16 ],
which further implies that the co-doping strategy with mixed-valence
ions at B-site is more potential to enhance the piezoelectricity of CBT-
based ceramics. However, related studies with above method in CBT-

ions at B-site is more potential to enhance the piezoelectricity of CBT-
based ceramics. However, related studies with above method in CBT-
based ceramic were rarely reported and the underlying enhancement
mechanism was still not well elucidated.
In this study, Nb – Mg co-doped CaBi Ti O ceramics are fabricated
by conventional solid-state reaction method and the e ﬀ ects of co-
doping on the structure and electrical properties of ceramics are
systematically explored. Optimized piezoelectric properties with a high
d value of 24 pC/N and a high T value of 787 °C along with a good
thermal stability are achieved. Related mechanisms for the enhanced
electrical performances are discussed rigorously.

4. Conclusions
In summary, mixed-valence ions Nb – Mg co-doped CaBi Ti (Nb
Mg ) O ( x = 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2) piezoceramics were prepared
by conventional solid-state method. Co-doping of Nb – Mg decreased the
oxygen concentration and led to increases in ferroelectricity and pie-
zoelectricity of CBT ceramics. A signi ﬁ cantly improved piezoelectric
properties were obtained with a high d value of 24 pC/N accompanied
by a high T of 787 °C. In addition, the resistivity and thermal stability
were also enhanced. These optimized electrical properties demon-
strated that the Nb – Mg co-doped CaBi Ti (Nb Mg ) O ceramics
could be a potential option for high temperature piezoelectric appli-
cations. It further implied that mixed valence ions doping at Ti-sites was
a doable way to improve the piezoelectricity of CBT ceramics.

Ce and W co-doped CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ceramics with chemical formula Ca 0.96 Ce 0.04 Bi 2 Nb 2- x W x O 9 (CCBN-
W100 x , x ¼ 0 e 0.07) are fabricated via conventional solid state sintering method, to investigate the effect
of W addition on the structure, electrical resistivity, dielectric and piezoelectric properties. A piezo-
electric constant d 33 of 13.4 pC/N is obtained in CCBN-W2 ceramics, > 100% higher than that of pure
CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ( d 33 ¼ 5.8 e 6.4 pC/N). Of particular signi ﬁ cance is that the electrical resistivity of CCBN-W2
ceramics ( r ¼ 3.7  10 U cm at 500 C) is three orders of magnitude higher than pure CaBi Nb O
( r ¼ 2.9  10 U cm at same temperature). All these properties, together with its low dielectric loss

ceramics ( r ¼ 3.7  10 U cm at 500 C) is three orders of magnitude higher than pure CaBi Nb O
( r ¼ 2.9  10 U cm at same temperature). All these properties, together with its low dielectric loss
(tan d ¼ 0.13%) and excellent d thermal stability up to 800 C, merit the CCBN-W2 ceramics for high

1. Introduction
Calcium bismuth niobate, CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 (CBN), is one of the most
actively studied compounds among Aurivillius-type bismuth layer-
structured ferroelectrics (BLSF) family [ 1 e 7 ]. CBN structure is
formed by one unit cell of CaNbO 3 with perovskite-like structure
interleaved with ﬂ uorite-like (Bi 2 O 2 ) 2 þ layers along the c -axis. The
ferroelectric to paraelectric phase transition temperature, i.e. Curie

interleaved with ﬂ uorite-like (Bi 2 O 2 ) 2 þ layers along the c -axis. The
ferroelectric to paraelectric phase transition temperature, i.e. Curie
temperature T c , is reported to be ~943 C for CBN. Because of such
high T c , CBN ceramics are good candidates for high-temperature
piezoelectric applications [ 8 e 10 ].
BLSF structure promotes a plate-like morphology, with platelets
growing preferentially in the fundamental plane ( a-b plane) [ 11 , 12 ].
Similar to many other compounds of BLSF family, the properties of
CBN show highly anisotropic [ 1 , 3 ]. Because the spontaneous po-
larization originates from different rotation modes of [NbO 6 ]
octahedral, the main component of polarization lies in the a-b
plane of perovskite-like CaNbO 3 layer. On the other hand, (Bi 2 O 2 ) 2 þ
layer, as a natural insulating medium, actually limits the charge
transport along the c -axis, leading to the in-plane maximum elec-
trical conductivity in the same a-b plane as the polarization [ 9 ]. As a

trical conductivity in the same a-b plane as the polarization [ 9 ]. As a
consequence, polycrystalline CBN ceramic sample is normally
dif ﬁ cult to pole to achieve full intrinsic performance, accounts for
the reported low piezoelectric constant d 33 ~6 pC/N [ 13 , 14 ].
Although a very high d 33 value of 19 pC/N can be obtained in CBN by
grain orientation technique, the markedly increased conductivity at
high temperature makes it unsuitable for practical application
[ 1 , 10 , 15 ]. Actually, in other textured BLSF ceramics, the resistivity
parallel to the texture direction (in a-b plane) has been reported
much lower than that perpendicular to the texture direction (along
the c -axis) [ 16 , 17 ].

2. Experimental
Cerium and tungsten co-doped CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 ceramics with
chemical formula Ca 0.96 Ce 0.04 Bi 2 Nb 2- x W x O 9 (CCBN-W100 x , x ¼ 0,
0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, and 0.07) were fabricated by conventional
processing route using raw materials of 99% CaCO 3 , 99.99% CeO 2 ,
99% Bi 2 O 3 , 99.99% Nb 2 O 5 , and 99.9% WO 3 (Sinopharm Chemical
Reagent Co. Ltd., Shanghai, China). The raw materials were weighed
according to nominal composition and mixed in a ball mill for 16 h,
using a polyethylene jar, zirconia balls and deionized water. The
mixture was calcined at 850 C for 3 h and then ball milled again for
16 h. After drying, the polyvinyl alcohol solution (PVA, 5 wt%) was
added in the calcined powders as a binder for granulation. Disks

1.  Introduction
High-temperature sensing based on the electromechanical
response of piezoelectric materials is of significant impor-
tance for the chemical engineering, automotive and aerospace
industries [ 1 , 2 ]. The ever-increasing demands on operational
temperature have spurred a tremendous research effort on high-
temperature piezoceramics. When an operational temper­ature
of 400 ° C or higher is required, bismuth layer-structured fer-
roelectrics (BLSFs) or Aurivillius-type piezoceramics seem
to be the only available materials because of their ultrahigh
Curie temperature ( T ) of around 600 – 900 ° C, in addition
to their low cost and non-toxicity [ 1 , 2 ]. BLSFs consist of
regular perovskite-like (A B O ) slabs separated
by (Bi O ) layers, where m is the number of perovskite-
like slabs. BLSFs also have low temperature coefficients of
resonance frequency, low aging rates, and excellent fatigue
endurance, etc. However, practical applications of BLSFs are

like slabs. BLSFs also have low temperature coefficients of
resonance frequency, low aging rates, and excellent fatigue
endurance, etc. However, practical applications of BLSFs are
severely limited due to their very low piezoelectricity and
difficulty of dense ceramic fabrication, because both sponta-
neous polarization (along the a - b plane) and mass transport
during sintering are restricted by their layered structure [ 3 , 4 ].
To resolve these problems, several strategies have been tried,
including composition adjustment (doping) [ 5 , 6 ], intergrowth

Abstract
We report an Aurivillius-type piezoelectric ceramic (Ca (LiCe) Bi Ti Zn O ) that has
an ultrahigh Curie temperature ( T ) around 800 ° C and a significantly enhanced piezoelectric
coefficient ( d ), comparable to that of textured ceramics fabricated using the complicated
templating method. Surprisingly, the highest d of 26 pC/N was achieved at an unexpectedly
low sintering temperature ( T ) of only 920 ° C (~200 ° C lower than usual) despite the non-ideal
density. Study of different synthesized samples indicates that a relatively low T is crucial

metadata.source: Cai 2017 J. Phys. D  Appl. Phys. 50 155302

text:
low sintering temperature ( T ) of only 920 ° C (~200 ° C lower than usual) despite the non-ideal
density. Study of different synthesized samples indicates that a relatively low T is crucial
for suppressing Bi evaporation and abnormal grain growth, which are indispensable for high
resistivity and effective poling due to decreased carrier density and restricted anisotropic
conduction. Because the layered structure is sensitive to lattice defects, controlled Bi loss is
considered to be crucial for maintaining structural order and spontaneous polarization. This
low- T system is very promising for practical applications due to its high piezoelectricity, low
cost and high reproducibility. Contrary to our usual understanding, the results reveal that a
delicate balance of density, Bi loss and grain morphology achieved by adjusting the sintering
temperature is crucial for the enhancing performance in Aurivillius-type high- T ceramics.

as low cost, ease of processing, low environmental pollu-

its application to BLSFs seems to be very rarely reported. In
contrast, a high sintering temperature is generally considered
to be necessary due to the difficulty of dense BLSF ceramic
fabrication [ 3 ]. CaBi Ti O (CBT) is a BLSF-type mat­erial
with a high T of about 790 ° C. However, compared to other

fabrication [ 3 ]. CaBi Ti O (CBT) is a BLSF-type mat­erial
with a high T of about 790 ° C. However, compared to other
m = 4 BLSF ceramics, e.g. K Bi Ti O ( T = 555 ° C,
d = 21.2 pC/N), CBT has a low d of only about 7 – 8
pC/N [ 17 ]. Here we report low-temperature sintered codoped
Ca (LiCe) Bi Ti Zn O ceramics using LiCO as a
raw additive that can also act as a sintering aid. Importantly,
due to its well-controlled composition and high resistivity, a
significantly increased d of 26 pC/N (about four times of
that of pure CBT) was obtained for an optimum composition
sintered at a temperature of only 920 ° C, which is 200 ° C
lower than those in existing reports [ 5 , 6 , 11 ]. This study
reveals that a delicate balance of density, Bi loss and grain
morphology at a relatively low sintering temperature is cru-
cial for enhancing the performance of Aurivillius-type high-
T ceramics. It may also provide some new hints on how to
enhance their performance.

2.  Experimental procedure
The study is focused on samples with a Li – Ce codoping
mole ratio of 0.025, which exhibit the highest d according
to experiments on different Ca (LiCe) Bi Ti Zn O
(hereafter referred to as CBT- x LiCe, x = 0 – 0.075) ceramics.
For sample preparation, a stoichiometric ratio of analyti-
cally pure CaCO , Bi O , Li CO , CeO , and commercial
grade TiO and ZnO powders were ball-milled in ethanol for
1000 min. Then the slurry was dried, ground, and calcined
at 800 ° C for 150 min. The final powders were mixed with
PVA and pressed into pellets with a diameter of ~10 mm
and a thickness of ~1 mm, and then sintered at temperatures
from 880 ° C to 1080 ° C. Densities were measured using the
Archimedes method. X-ray diffraction (XRD) profiles were
characterized by a Bruker D8 Advance diffractometor with

metadata.source: Cai 2017 J. Phys. D  Appl. Phys. 50 155302

text:
from 880 ° C to 1080 ° C. Densities were measured using the
Archimedes method. X-ray diffraction (XRD) profiles were
characterized by a Bruker D8 Advance diffractometor with
Cu K α 1 radiation. The morphology of the fresh fractured
surfaces of the samples was examined by scanning electron
microscopy (SEM, Hitachi S-4800, Japan). Ceramic com-
positions were also derived by comparing the x-ray fluores-
cence (XRF) peak intensity of the elements using a Skyray
EDX3600B instrument. The temperature dependence of
the dielectric constant ε (1 kHz – 1 MHz) of unpoled sam-
ples with silver electrodes was measured using a HP4294A
impedance analyzer. After poling at 180 ° C for 20 min under
an electric field of about 9 kV mm in silicone oil, d
values were tested using a ZJ-3A type d meter (Institute of
Acoustics, Chinese Academy of Sciences). The mechanical
quality factor ( Q ) and planar electromechanical coupling
factor ( K ) were measured via the resonance – anti-resonance

metadata.source: Cai 2017 J. Phys. D  Appl. Phys. 50 155302

text:
Acoustics, Chinese Academy of Sciences). The mechanical
quality factor ( Q ) and planar electromechanical coupling
factor ( K ) were measured via the resonance – anti-resonance
method using the impedance analyzer. In situ high-temper­
ature k values were derived by the same method at each
temper­ature. The polarization hysteresis loops were measured
using a Radiant Precision LC ferroelectric testing system.
A HP4140B pA Meter with a HP16055A Test Fixture was
used to measure resistivity. Thermal depolarization experi-
ments were also conducted by annealing poled samples at
various temperatures for 1 h and then measuring the room
temperature d .

3.  Results and discussion
The d values of the CBT- x LiCe samples that were sintered
at different temperatures are shown in figure 1 . The samples
show d in the range of 8 to 26 pC/N. A very interesting
phenom­enon is that, for all compositions, the maximum d
was achieved at only 920 ° C – 960 ° C, while the highest d was
obtained in the CBT-0.025LiCe sample that was sintered at
920 ° C, which is about 200 ° C lower than the usually reported
data [ 5 , 6 , 11 ]. This is surprising because a high T is gener-
ally accepted to be indispensable for high density and strong
piezoelectricity, while such a low T is very desirable for
industrial applications due to the associated much lower cost
and higher reproducibility. The highest d of CBT-0.025LiCe
(26 pC/N) is about four times of that of pure CBT and com-
parable to textured CBT that is fabricated with a much more
complicated procedure [ 11 ]. Therefore, we focus on this com-
position. Other electrical parameters of the optimum samples,

4.  Conclusions
An Aurivillius-type piezoelectric ceramic (Ca (LiCe) Bi
Ti Zn O ) with an ultrahigh Curie temperature ( T ) of
about 800 ° C and a significantly enhanced piezoelectric coeffi-
cient ( d ) comparable to those of textured ceramics was fabri-
cated. Surprisingly, the highest d of 26 pC N was achieved
at a relatively low sintering temperature ( T ) of only 920 ° C
despite its density not being the highest. A relatively low T
was found to be crucial for reducing Bi evaporation and sup-
pressing abnormal grain growth, which are indispensable for
high resistivity and effective poling due to decreased carrier
density and restricted anisotropic conduction. Considering
that the layered structure is sensitive to defects, we propose
that controlled Bi loss is crucial for maintaining large polar-
ization. This low- T system is very promising for industrial

metadata.source: Cai 2017 J. Phys. D  Appl. Phys. 50 155302

text:
that the layered structure is sensitive to defects, we propose
that controlled Bi loss is crucial for maintaining large polar-
ization. This low- T system is very promising for industrial
applications due to its enhanced piezoelectricity, low cost
and high reproducibility. Contrary to the usual strategies of
increasing density, this study reveals that a delicate balance
of density, Bi loss and grain morphology by adjusting the
sinter­ing temperature is very effective for enhancing the per-
formance of Aurivillius-type high- T ceramics.

A B S T R A C T
As the industry advances at a swift pace, the demand for piezoelectric materials that exhibit both exceptional
piezoelectric properties and excellent thermal stability is on the rise. However, it remains a significant challenge
to achieve a balance between high piezoelectricity and thermal stability in these materials. In this study, the
phase structure, microstructure, and thermal stability of Ce-doped CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 (CLBBN- x Ce) high-temperature
bismuth layer-structured piezoceramics are studied. It is revealed that the CLBBN-0.1Ce ceramics stand out
with a piezoelectric coefficient d 33 of 21.7 pC/N and a high Curie temperature of 907 C. Furthermore, in situ
temperature measurement demonstrates that the d 33 has a change rate of 20.8 % from room temperature to 400

temperature measurement demonstrates that the d 33 has a change rate of 20.8 % from room temperature to 400
C. We found that grain size refinement and domain morphology contribute to excellent electrical properties of
the Ce-doped CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 -based ceramics. The superior performance of these ceramics suggests they hold great
promise for high-temperature applications.
1. Introduction
Piezoelectric materials are widely used in sensors, actuators and
transducers, due to their ability to realize the mutual conversion of
electrical and mechanical energies [1 – 5] . As industries such as aero­
space, nuclear power, and automotive manufacturing progress at a rapid
pace, there is a growing need for piezoelectric materials that can operate
at higher temperatures and exhibit enhanced thermal stability [6 – 11] .
Piezoelectric coefficient ( d 33 ) is one of the most important parameters to
measure the piezoelectric properties of materials, and its value is sen­

Piezoelectric coefficient ( d 33 ) is one of the most important parameters to
measure the piezoelectric properties of materials, and its value is sen­
sitive to temperature fluctuations. When the environmental temperature
exceeds the Curie temperature ( T C ) of piezoelectric ceramics, the crystal
structure will change from an asymmetric configuration to a symmet­
rical configuration, which leads to the loss of piezoelectric functionality.
To maintain the safety and reliability of piezoelectric ceramics, their
operational temperature is usually limited to below 50 % of the Curie
temperature, which significantly curtails their potential applications
[12 – 14] . Therefore, the development of piezoelectric ceramics that offer
a high piezoelectric coefficient, a high Curie temperature, and superior
thermal stability has emerged as a key research objective in the quest for
high-temperature piezoelectric ceramics.

4. Conclusions
The CLBBN- x Ce ceramics, with varying Ce concentrations ( x = 0,
0.05, 0.1, 0.15, and 0.2), were synthesized by the solid-state reaction
method. The systematical study results reveal the impact of Ce-doping
on the electric properties and thermal stability of CBN-based ceramics.
It is noteworthy that the CLBBN-0.1Ce ceramic exhibits a maximum d 33
value of 21.7 pC/N, complemented by a high Curie temperature of 907

It is noteworthy that the CLBBN-0.1Ce ceramic exhibits a maximum d 33
value of 21.7 pC/N, complemented by a high Curie temperature of 907
C. In the in situ temperature-dependent d 33 measurements, from room
temperature to 400 C, the rate of change of d 33 of CLBBN-0.1Ce samples
is 20.8 %, which is also an important attribute for practical applications.
The results of this study highlight the significant advantages of the Ce-
doped CLBBN ceramics, suggesting their promising potential for appli­
cation in high-temperature environments. These ceramics stand out as
robust candidates for applications where both high thermal stability and
superior piezoelectric properties are concurrently demanded.

Two-layer structured ferroelectric ceramics, Ca (NaBi) Bi Nb O ( x = 0.0 – 0.5; CNBN- x ), were prepared by
solid-state sintering. An arti ﬁ cial pseudo-morphotropic phase boundary was formed by the substitution of Ca
with NaBi, and the crystal structure tended to crystallise in the pseudo-tetragonal phase as the increase of NaBi
content. Curie temperature ( T ) slightly reduce and remain high value with the increase of NaBi content, which
is in the range of 880 – 935 °C. Moreover, enhanced piezoactivity ( d ) and ferroelectricity ( P ) accompanying
with decreased dielectric loss can be acquired in NaBi-modi ﬁ ed CaBi Nb O The CNBN-0.1 had the best per-
formance, and its T , d and P was 925 °C, 14.4 pC/N and 6.0 μ C/cm , respectively. Thermal annealing
measurement exhibited that the piezoelectric properties of Ca (NaBi) Bi Nb O had good temperature sta-

measurement exhibited that the piezoelectric properties of Ca (NaBi) Bi Nb O had good temperature sta-
bility up to 800 °C. Therefore, the NaBi-modi ﬁ ed CaBi Nb O ceramics are perceived to be of promising can-
didates for high-temperature applications.
1. Introduction
Piezoelectric sensors at high temperature such as accelerometers,
high temperature SAW (Surface Acoustic Wave) sensors, acoustic
emission sensors and gas/pressure sensors, etc. are widely used to de-
tect and record dynamic mechanical parameters at harsh conditions for
structural control and health monitoring system in the ﬁ elds of aircraft,
aerospace and nuclear power industries [1 – 4] . Take the aircraft and
aerospace industry as an example, the piezoelectric accelerometers are
usually required to be the closest approach to the engine components
for su ﬃ cient detection sensitivity to e ﬀ ectively monitor the working
situation of the engine, which demands devices can endure high tem-

for su ﬃ cient detection sensitivity to e ﬀ ectively monitor the working
situation of the engine, which demands devices can endure high tem-
peratures more than 500 °C [4] . This indicates that the piezoelectric
materials must be able to function well and have very good thermal
stability in a wide temperature range since they are the key component
of high-temperature piezoelectric sensors.
From the viewpoint of piezoelectric sensors, the maximum opera-
tion temperature is restricted by both Curie temperature ( T ) and sen-
sitivity level, which is settled by the piezoelectric coe ﬃ cients, the
electrical resistivity and the dielectric losses of piezoelectric materials
[5] . Aurivillius-type piezoceramics, with the general chemical formula

conduces to charge drift disturbing the formation of piezoelectrically

Two-layer Aurivillius phase piezoelectric ceramics, MBi Nb O (M
represents the A-site cation), have attracted signi ﬁ cant research inter-
ests from the technological and scienti ﬁ c points of view due to their
unique overall performance. Among them, CaBi Nb O (CBN, m =2) is
prospective for high-temperature piezoelectric sensor applications be-
cause that it has the highest-known T of 943 °C [9] . However, the
piezoelectric coe ﬃ cient ( d ) of pure CBN ceramic is relatively low ( ∼
6 pC/N) [10] . Meanwhile, Na Bi Nb O (NBN, m =2) is also a ty-

piezoelectric coe ﬃ cient ( d ) of pure CBN ceramic is relatively low ( ∼

(790 °C), but relatively low piezoelectric coe ﬃ cient (~6 pC/N) [11] .
Many approaches have been carried out to enhance the piezoelectric
properties of CBN and NBN ceramics via texture techniques (such as
spark plasma sintering [9] , templated grain growth [12] , hot pressing
[13] etc.) and/or cation doping modi ﬁ cations [14,15] . It was found that

2. Experimental procedure
Ceramic samples with compositions of Ca (NaBi) Bi Nb O
( x = 0.0, 0.1, 0.3, and 0.5, abbreviated as CBN, CNBN-0.1, CNBN-0.3
and CNBN-0.5, respectively) were prepared using the solid-state sin-
tering. The starting raw materials are CaCO (99.00%), Na CO
(98.92%), Bi O (99.78%) and Nb O (99.95%). All raw materials were
weighed in the stoichiometric ratio and planetary milling for 4 h.
Calcination of dried powders was performed at 850 °C for 2 h after
which ball-milling again for 4 h under the same conditions was carried
out. The dried powders with 7 wt% binder (polyvinyl alcohol) were
pressed into pellets. The pellets were maintained at 750 °C for 2 h to

out. The dried powders with 7 wt% binder (polyvinyl alcohol) were
pressed into pellets. The pellets were maintained at 750 °C for 2 h to
remove the binder. All samples were sintered at 1100 °C for 2 h and
then processed into to the same size (12 mm in diameter, 0.5 mm in
thickness) for performance measurements.
X-ray di ﬀ raction (XRD) patterns of Ca (NaBi) Bi Nb O cera-
mics were obtained by X-ray di ﬀ ractometer (D/max2550V, Rigaku, Co.,
Tokyo, Japan) with Cu K α radiation. Natural microstructures were
examined by using scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Hitachi, Tokyo,
Japan). Raman spectra were measured by using micro-Raman spec-
trometer (Jobin-Yvon Lab RAW HR 800 UV) equipped with the exciting
source with the 632.8 nm line from He-Ne laser. In order to measure
electrical properties, the platinum paste was coated on the two surfaces
of the samples. Dielectric properties were characterised by E4980A LCR
meter. Ferroelectric properties measurements were performed by using

of the samples. Dielectric properties were characterised by E4980A LCR
meter. Ferroelectric properties measurements were performed by using
TF-2000 ferroelectric analyser (aixACCT, Aachen, Germany). DC elec-
trical resistivity measurement was carried out by using the resistivity
test system HRMS-900 (Partulab, Wuhan, China) in the range of
200 – 700 °C. All ceramics samples were polarised by applying di ﬀ erent
dc electric ﬁ elds for 20 min in silicone oil bath of 200 °C. The d were
measured by a quasi-static ZJ-6 d meter (Institute of Acoustics,
Chinese Academy of Sciences, China). Temperature stability of piezo-
electric properties of all the compositions was achieved by post-an-
nealing the polarised samples at di ﬀ erent temperatures for 4 h, and re-
measuring d when the samples were cooled to room temperature. The
above procedure was repeated at various temperatures until 950 °C.

1. Introduction
Piezoelectric ceramic materials are a kind of important functional
materials to realize electromechanical energy conversion and cou-
pling. Using the positive piezoelectric effect of mechanical vibration
converted into electrical signal, it can be used to manufacture pie-
zoelectric pickup, buzzer, and ultrasonic receiving probe [1–4] .
Conversely, by converting the AC signal into the inverse piezoelectric
effect of mechanical vibration, it can be used to manufacture ultra-

Conversely, by converting the AC signal into the inverse piezoelectric
effect of mechanical vibration, it can be used to manufacture ultra-
sonic emitters, piezoelectric speakers, and ultrasonic cleaning
agents [5–8] .
In the current practical application, lead zirconate titanate (PZT)
occupies a dominant position, but its curie temperature ( T ) is gen-
erally maintained at about 350 °C, so the temperature of PZT working
stably for a long time is also around 170 °C, and serious depolarization
will occur when the ambient temperature is higher than 170 °C.
Moreover, lead is easy to volatilize at high temperature, which will
also pollute the environment and cause damage to human body.
Therefore, lead-free piezoelectric materials that can work normally in
a wider temperature range have become a research hotspot. The
general structural formula of bismuth layer structured ferroelectrics
(BLSFs) discovered by Aurivillius is (Bi O ) (A B O ) [9] , the

4. Conclusion
Bismuth layer structured ferroelectrics (BLSFs) Bi (Li Ln )
TiNbO (BTNO-1LiLn, Ln = La, Nd, Gd, and Er) high temperature pie-
zoelectric ceramics were synthesized by solid state reaction sintering,

Bismuth layer structured ferroelectrics (BLSFs) Bi (Li Ln )
TiNbO (BTNO-1LiLn, Ln = La, Nd, Gd, and Er) high temperature pie-
zoelectric ceramics were synthesized by solid state reaction sintering,
and their microstructure and electrical properties were studied in
detail. It is found that BTNO-1LiLa has excellent anti depolarization
performance due to the difference in the occupation of La and other
Ln (Nd , Gd , and Er ) in BTNO. However, the special occupation
of La makes O3 in bismuth layer seriously deteriorate the sponta-
neous polarization ( P ), and the larger ion radius of La makes the
overall distortion of BO6 octahedron along the a -axis smaller, re-
sulting in the piezoelectric coefficient ( d ) of BTNO-1LiLa is only
7.6 pC/N, while that of BTNO-1LiEe reached 10.6 pC/N. Finally, based
on the first principle, the band structure of BTNO pure ceramic is
calculated by Materials Studio, and the band gap ( E ) is 2.143 eV, while
the activation energy ( E ) of BTNO-1LiLn is between 0.7 eV ~ 0.9 eV,

calculated by Materials Studio, and the band gap ( E ) is 2.143 eV, while
the activation energy ( E ) of BTNO-1LiLn is between 0.7 eV ~ 0.9 eV,
which shows that the introduction of (Li Ln ) in BTNO will
transform it into p -type semiconductor, and the conductivity is rea-
lized by the movement of electron holes. This work provides theo-
retical support for the design of high temperature piezoelectric
ceramics with better performance in the future.
